Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 1–2:

Ta-Sin-Mim. ...That is the Clear Book. (2)

The purpose of mentioning the letters of the alphabet is to show that this Clear Book, and this surah, have been composed from these very letters. The letters are known to those who insist on denying, and they speak words formed from them, yet they cannot produce a Clear Book like this. Many matters concerning this Book are discussed in this surah, both in its introduction and in its final conclusions. This is the style of all those surahs that begin with the disjointed letters (huruf muqatta'at).

After this warning, the Prophet is addressed directly, because he was striving tirelessly against the polytheists, and their continuous denial was causing him grief. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is consoled here and told not to be too distressed over this matter. It is said: it is true that you are bearing a great deal, and it is also true that if We wished, We could bring their necks low in an instant, but Allah has a plan. Wait a while.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 3–4:

لعلک باخع ……خضعین (4)

The style of address is such that it is as though the Prophet ﷺ himself is being admonished not to endanger his life because these people do not believe.

لعلک باخع نفسک (26:3) "Perhaps you will destroy yourself with grief." The phrase "bakhi' al-nafs" means "killing the self." This shows how deeply distressed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was at the non-belief of the Quraysh of Makkah. He was certain that if they did not believe, they might be destroyed like the other nations, and so he was consuming himself in this grief. The reality is that these people were his relatives, his family, and his own people, and this made him all the more anxious. But the Lord, Exalted is He, had greater compassion for him than he had for himself. Allah forbade him from this destructive heartache, saying that he should continue his work with ease and tranquility. It is not his duty that people believe. If only the belief of people had been desired, We could have bent their necks with a single command. We would have sent down from the heavens a sign such that they would bow their heads, there would be no way to refuse, and they could not turn away from faith, and they would be left cowed and subdued at once.

فظلت اعنا قھم لھا خضعین (26:4) "Then their necks would remain bowed before it." These people would stand with bowed necks, as though bound, unable to move from their place. They would stand with hands folded in submission.

But it was not Allah's will to compel these people to accept this final Messenger. Only one miracle was given to this Messenger, and that miracle was the Qur'an. This Qur'an provides a complete system of life, and it is a miracle in every respect. It is only necessary to advance and accept it.

This Qur'an is also miraculous in its manner of expression and its artistic order and arrangement. Throughout the whole Qur'an, this speech maintains its high standard and elevated level. In terms of artistry, eloquence and rhetorical power, there is no decline or dip in it. That is, nowhere does the speech fall below its standard, and nowhere has it abandoned its distinctive qualities. It is not like human speech, in which highs and lows keep appearing: sometimes lofty, sometimes middling, and sometimes plainly low; sometimes grand and sometimes flat. For example, a single author speaks in one manner in one place and changes his style in another. But the Qur'an flows like a stream from beginning to end, on one level, at one pace, and at one standard, which shows that its source is also one.

Then, in terms of its ideas and doctrines, it is also a miracle. Its intellectual components are interconnected. There is not a single statement in it that does not fit with its overall framework, and there is no contradiction. All its guidance and all its codifications are complete and harmonious according to one single system. These teachings encompass the whole life of a human being. The full range of life's problems is addressed in it, and the complete answer to all the problems of human life is present in it. Not one of its particulars opposes or contradicts any other particular of the Qur'an. Moreover, this entire intellectual system is in harmony with the natural order. All components of thought revolve around one axis; everything is bound on one cord, with complete harmony. Man, with his limited ability, is not capable of presenting such an integrated system of thought and action. Therefore, it is a system sent down by the Absolute Expert, and it is beyond the limits of time and space. In short, the system of the Qur'an possesses such comprehensiveness, and its intellectual and practical organization is astonishing.

Furthermore, there is another miracle within it: as soon as its voice is heard, it penetrates the hearts; it holds the keys to hearts.

As soon as one hears it, hearts open up, and the hidden powers within a person that receive impressions awaken and respond to its call. It resolves tangled religious questions with such simplicity and ease that a person is left astonished, without any difficulty, complexity, or excessive effort. With just a single utterance, it transforms the world of hearts.

Allah's will required that the Qur'an be designated as a miracle for this final Messenger, and Allah did not consider it appropriate to send down a material and physical miracle which, upon seeing it, would bend people's necks so that they would accept it out of compulsion. This is because this final prophethood was a general and open message for all humanity, a guidance for future generations until the Day of Resurrection, and it was not a message confined to one nation or bound to a limited time. Therefore, Allah gave this Messenger a miracle that is universal for both distant and near nations, for every people and every generation. As for material miracles, only those who witness them bow before them, and after those nations, such events become stories and narratives; they are not a visible sign for future generations.

As for the noble Qur'an, it has been a miracle for fourteen hundred years. It is an open book and a powerful system of life. If the people of any age take it as their guide and leader, they can benefit from it; it can resolve all the problems of their lives, fulfill their needs, and indeed lead them to the best life and the finest outcomes at a most exalted level. It is a treasure such that whatever we have not discovered from it in our age, future generations will discover. It gives every seeker according to his question, and gives generously, and its treasures never run out; rather, new stores are constantly found anew. But people are such that they do not attain the great treasures and wisdoms of this Qur'an, and they turn away. Whenever a new verse of the Qur'an was revealed, they would say:

Here, among the Names of Allah, al-Rahman (the Most Gracious) is brought forward. This points to the fact that by sending down this Book and this admonition, Allah has shown a very great mercy to His creatures, and yet they are turning away from that mercy. It is therefore obvious that their conduct is extremely abominable and disgraceful. Mercy is descending upon them from the heavens, and they are fleeing from it. They are depriving themselves of Allah's bounty, which they truly stand in great need of.

For this reason, a very severe warning is revealed from Allah regarding their turning away: the punishment of Allah awaits them. Very soon they will be confronted with it.

Therefore they have indeed denied, so there will come to them the news of that which they used to mock. (26:6)

Note: the phrase "فقد ……یستھزء ون (6)" in the original is the verse reference, and the verse itself is rendered below.

And this threat is extremely veiled and ambiguous, and the punishment is left unspecified. Since these people considered these threats a joke, Allah also made the manner of the threat mocking.

﴿So they will soon learn the truth of that which they used to mock at.﴾ (26:6) That is, news of the punishment which they mock will reach them. Not merely will the news of this punishment reach these people, but they will also taste the punishment, and they themselves will become a news item. The calamity that befalls them will be recounted by people in the streets and lanes to one another. Since they were mocking, the reply in this threat is also given in a mocking manner. Yet this mockery is full of threat.

These people demand a miracle that breaks natural custom, and they take no notice of the clear, bright, and shining signs and miracles of Allah that are spread around them. In the presence of these signs and manifestations, a conquered heart and a sensitive insight need no further proof or demonstration. The page of this universe is so wondrous that the human heart and mind are satisfied upon beholding it.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 7–8:

اولم ……مئومنین (8)

1033

To bring forth from this dead earth a kind of living vegetation is itself no small miracle. Then, to make from these plants male and female: in some species the male and female are on separate plants, while in others the male and female flowers are on a single plant, as is the case in most vegetation, meaning that the male and female parts are found on one and the same branch. And this miracle takes place around them day and night.

﴿Have they not seen?﴾ (26:8). These are miracles for which a single act of observation is enough. It is a distinctive feature of the Qur'anic method of education that the Qur'an invites the human heart and mind to reflect upon the observation of this universe. The Qur'an awakens a dulled sensibility, sharpens a dull mind, and frees the faculties of perception that have been shut, and draws them to the miracles present in this universe, which are scattered at every step, so that a person may look at this universe with a living heart and mind. He should see the wondrous creations of God, gain awareness of God, and attain knowledge of God through the wondrous creatures of God. He should remain constantly fearful of God, and have the consciousness that God is watching. Then every human being should be aware that, among God's creatures, he alone is the one who possesses this awareness, and who is also connected to God's creatures and bound to this law of nature (fitrah) which God has made to operate throughout this universe. Then he should also be aware that he has a particular role to play in this universe, especially with regard to this earth, upon whose shoulders a specific responsibility has been placed.

﴿Have they not looked at the earth, how We have caused to grow in it every noble kind of pair?﴾ (26:7). These are most excellent, because life is within them, and this life has been placed in them by the Lord, the Most Generous. By the word "Karim" (noble/generous), God conveys the impression that His works of creation should be viewed with the greatest attention, significance and reverence. These are not ordinary realities that one should pass over like a heedless and ignorant person.

﴿Indeed in that is a sign﴾ (26:8). What need then remains to seek further signs beyond these? Yet these people do not believe in these ordinary signs.

﴿And most of them are not believers﴾ (26:8). The introduction of this surah concludes with this instructive phrase, which is repeated again and again throughout the surah.

. "That is, He is Almighty (al-'Aziz) and has power over the creation of every kind of wondrous creature, over displaying every kind of miracle, and over punishing those who deny and reject. And He is also Merciful (al-Rahim): in His Book He presents to people some of His creatures and these marvels and wonders, and He also points out the proofs and signs. In this way, those whose hearts are inclined towards guidance believe. Moreover, He grants respite to those who deny, and He does not punish them until He sends a messenger who gives a clear message. Yet the signs of this universe are present in very great abundance, and no further proof or argument is needed. But it is the mercy of Allah that He also sends messengers to illuminate people's consciences, to provide them with insight, to give them the good news of a good end, and to warn them of a bad end; therefore He is Merciful and Generous."

Lesson No. 162: At a Glance

The portion of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) given here is closely aligned with the theme and central focus of this surah. The main concern of this surah is what the end of those who deny (al-mukadhdhibin) turns out to be. Moreover, in this surah too, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is consoled, and sympathy is expressed for the difficulties he faced as a result of the aversion and denial of the polytheists. Another theme of this surah is the assurance that Allah is the supporter, helper and protector of this call and of the movement that carries it, even though its followers are weak while their opponents are equipped with resources (zad wa 'ttad, i.e., provisions and equipment), are powerful and tyrannical, and are inflicting oppression upon them. For at the time this surah was revealed, the Islamic movement in Makkah was passing through exactly such conditions. The stories of earlier prophets are an important material and a means of training within the educational method of the Qur'an.

Some links of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) have already passed in Surah al-Baqarah, Surah al-Ma'idah, Surah al-A'raf, Surah Yunus, Surah al-Isra, Surah al-Kahf and Surah Ta-Ha, while in some other surahs there are also brief allusions to the life of Musa (peace be upon him).

Wherever a link of this story has been alluded to, or a link has been given in detail, that link and that portion have been most fitting to the subject under discussion; in every place the appropriate portion has been brought in accordance with the context of the speech. Just as the links in this story are proportionate to the theme of this surah and clarify the same purpose. (For details see Fi Zilal, Para Six.)

The section given here relates to prophethood and its denial. The events of denial, and of the plot against Musa and his companions, leading to the drowning of Pharaoh and his people are presented, and it is explained that Musa and his companions were delivered from the clutches of the oppressors. Thus this entire link is a confirmation of the verse:

﴿وَسَيَعْلَمُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا أَيَّ مُنقَلَبٍ يَنقَلِبُونَ﴾ (26:227) "And those who have done wrong will soon know what final return they will be returned to." It is also a confirmation of Allah's saying:

﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبُوا فَسَيَأْتِيهِمْ أَنبَاءُ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ (26:6) "So they have denied, and the news of what they used to mock will soon reach them."

This portion of the story of Musa consists of several scenes which needed to be shown. Between these scenes there are gaps and intervals in which the curtain on the scene falls, and when it rises again, the next scene is before the eyes. This is the feature that has been preserved throughout the Qur'an when presenting stories.

In this link there are seven scenes. In the first scene, a call comes from Allah. Musa converses with his Lord, is honoured with the office of prophethood, and revelation comes to him. In the second scene, Kalim (the Interlocutor) and Pharaoh come face to face. Pharaoh's courtiers are also present there. Musa presents the message, and the miracles of the staff and the luminous hand are shown. In the third scene, the magicians are brought against Musa. People gather in a vast field and there is discussion of the opponent's plans. In the fourth scene, the magicians are gathered in Pharaoh's court and are receiving firm promises of reward and honour if they win the field. The fifth scene is the scene of the contest: the contest takes place, the magicians believe, and Pharaoh threatens them. In the sixth scene there are glimpses of both camps: on one side is the scene of divine revelation, where Musa is commanded by Allah to prepare and to leave by night with My servants; on the other side Pharaoh sends his agents to all the regions and armies are assembled. In the seventh scene, the pursuing army and the fleeing believers stand before a sea. The sea splits, and through those watery paths the oppressed pass across while the oppressors are drowned.

These same scenes are presented in Surah al-A'raf, Surah Yunus and Surah Ta-Ha as well. But in each place the manner and colouring of the story differ, and the story is brought in the manner of the direction in which the discourse is heading. Thus the aspect of the story that is related to the subject under discussion is highlighted.

In Surah al-A'raf the story begins directly with a brief dialogue between Kalim and Pharaoh. Then a glimpse of the contest with the magicians is shown, while the plots and intrigues of Pharaoh and his chiefs are shown well and in detail, and between the contest with the magicians and the drowning of Pharaoh's army, Musa is brought on the scene showing miracles in Egypt. Then, when this army passes safely through the sea, several phases of life of migration are presented. Here in this surah, however, these links have been omitted, and the dialogue between Musa and Pharaoh on the subject of tawhid is given at length, because this is the theme of this surah, and this very dialogue is at its height between the polytheists of Makkah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In Surah Yunus the story begins with a brief dialogue between Kalim and Pharaoh, the miracles of the staff and the luminous hand are not shown, and the details of the dialogue with the magicians are also omitted; whereas here both are brought in detail. In Ta-Ha, the intimate conversation between Musa and the Lord the Exalted is brought in detail. Then the encounter of Musa and Pharaoh and the contest with the magicians are cursory, while the migration journey of the Children of Israel is detailed. Here the scenes of the story end with the drowning of Pharaoh.

Thus, when we find this story repeatedly in various surahs of the Qur'an, the artistry of the Qur'anic style appears before us: nowhere do we see that it is the same story being repeated, because in each place different links are shown, different scenes are presented, one particular aspect of the story is opened up and explained, and the manner of expression is new each time. All these features make the story new in every place, and in every place the story is also in harmony with its subject.

Lesson No. 162: Explanation of the Verses

10 to 68

﴿وَإِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبُّكَ مُوسَىٰ أَنِ ائْتِ الْقَوْمَ الظَّالِمِينَ * قَوْمَ فِرْعَوْنَ أَلَا يَتَّقُونَ﴾ (26:10-11) "And [mention] when your Lord called Musa: 'Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear Allah?'" This is the first scene of the story here. In it, Musa (peace be upon him) is given the office of prophethood and a mission. He is told that he has to go to a wrongdoing people. They first wronged themselves, being afflicted with disbelief and misguidance. Then they wronged the Children of Israel, for they keep their women alive and slaughter their men, mock them at every turn, and inflict all kinds of punishments upon them. After first describing the qualities of this people, their name is now mentioned: go to the people of Pharaoh. Musa and all humanity are amazed: will this wrongdoing people not fear their evil end? Do they not fear Allah? Do they not know the consequence of their oppressions? Will these people not desist even after such abominable crimes? Their case is strange and astonishing, and so is the case of every such people who exceed all limits.

The case of Pharaoh and his people was not new to Musa (peace be upon him); he knew them well. He was well aware of Pharaoh's oppression, his tyranny and his arrogance, and knew well that this was a great and difficult mission entrusted to him.

For this reason, he places his weaknesses before his Lord. Not because he wished to shrink from this call or to make a permanent excuse, but because he sought the further necessary help and support for this mission.

﴿قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي أَخَافُ أَن يُكَذِّبُونِ * وَيَضِيقُ صَدْرِي وَلَا يَنطَلِقُ لِسَانِي فَأَرْسِلْ إِلَىٰ هَارُونَ * وَلَهُمْ عَلَيَّ ذَنبٌ فَأَخَافُ أَن يَقْتُلُونِ﴾ (26:12-14) He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me. My chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed, so send to Harun. And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."

Here the words of Musa (peace be upon him) that are quoted apparently show that he speaks these words merely out of fear of denial, but he is being given prophethood in circumstances where there is a tightness in his heart and he does not have fluency of speech. In the matter of prophethood he will have to debate and converse with everyone, and his condition is that there is a stammer in his tongue, and he has stated this explicitly in Surah Ta-Ha:

﴿وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي * يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي﴾ (20:27-28) "And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech."

When a person has a stammer in his tongue, a tightness arises in his chest because of it. This tightness is extremely painful when a person wants to speak and wants to express arguments along with his feelings, and the tongue abandons him at that very moment. As the flood of thoughts and emotions surges, the tongue shuts and the heart constricts, and the person's condition becomes pitiable to see. Everyone has seen this state. Therefore Musa (peace be upon him) is anxious that if in such circumstances his tongue were to be tied up, it would be a very strange position, especially when the confrontation is with a tyrant and oppressor like Pharaoh. So he placed his weakness before his Lord, and at the same time made the request that Harun be also granted the station of prophethood, that he be made a partner in this office, so that both of them together might perform this great duty. The purpose was not that Musa (peace be upon him) was hesitating to accept this office or wished to shirk it. Lesson No. 162: At a Glance

The portion of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) given here is closely aligned with the theme and central focus of this surah. The main concern of this surah is what the end of those who deny (al-mukadhdhibin) turns out to be. Another theme of this surah is the assurance that Allah is the supporter, helper and protector of this call and of the movement that carries it, even though its followers are weak while their opponents are equipped with resources (zad wa 'ttad, i.e., provisions and equipment), are powerful and tyrannical, and are inflicting oppression upon them. For at the time this surah was revealed, the Islamic movement in Makkah was passing through exactly such conditions. The stories of earlier prophets are an important material and a means of training within the educational method of the Qur'an.

Some links of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) have already passed in Surah al-Baqarah, Surah al-Ma'idah, Surah al-A'raf, Surah Yunus, Surah al-Isra, Surah al-Kahf and Surah Ta-Ha, while in some other surahs there are also brief allusions to the life of Musa (peace be upon him).

Wherever a link of this story has been alluded to, or a link has been given in detail, that link and that portion have been most fitting to the subject under discussion; in every place the appropriate portion has been brought in accordance with the context of the speech. Just as the links in this story are proportionate to the theme of this surah and clarify the same purpose. (For details see Fi Zilal, Para Six.)

The section given here relates to prophethood and its denial. The events of denial, and of the plot against Musa and his companions, leading to the drowning of Pharaoh and his people are presented, and it is explained that Musa and his companions were delivered from the clutches of the oppressors. ﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبُوا فَسَيَأْتِيهِمْ أَنبَاءُ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ (26:6) "So they have denied, and the news of what they used to mock will soon reach them."

This portion of the story of Musa consists of several scenes which needed to be shown. In this link there are seven scenes. In the first scene, a call comes from Allah. Musa converses with his Lord, is honoured with the office of prophethood, and revelation comes to him. In the second scene, Kalim (the Interlocutor) and Pharaoh come face to face. Pharaoh's courtiers are also present there. Musa presents the message, and the miracles of the staff and the luminous hand are shown. In the third scene, the magicians are brought against Musa. People gather in a vast field and there is discussion of the opponent's plans. In the fourth scene, the magicians are gathered in Pharaoh's court and are receiving firm promises of reward and honour if they win the field. The fifth scene is the scene of the contest: the contest takes place, the magicians believe, and Pharaoh threatens them. In the sixth scene there are glimpses of both camps: on one side is the scene of divine revelation, where Musa is commanded by Allah to prepare and to leave by night with My servants; on the other side Pharaoh sends his agents to all the regions and armies are assembled. In the seventh scene, the pursuing army and the fleeing believers stand before a sea. The sea splits, and through those watery paths the oppressed pass across while the oppressors are drowned.

The stage of the acceptance of the prayer here is extremely brief. The making of Harun a prophet, Musa's arrival in Egypt, and his meeting with Harun have been omitted, and only this is shown: Musa and Harun, both carrying the commands of their Lord, are preparing to converse with Pharaoh. But Musa's apprehensions are checked with only one strong word, which carries the sense of "no" and is meant as a warning:

﴿كَلَّا﴾ "By no means."

Lesson No. 162: At a Glance

The portion of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) given here is closely aligned with the theme and central focus of this surah. The main concern of this surah is what the end of those who deny (al-mukadhdhibin) turns out to be. Moreover, in this surah too, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is consoled, and sympathy is expressed for the difficulties he faced as a result of the aversion and denial of the polytheists. Another theme of this surah is the assurance that Allah is the supporter, helper and protector of this call and of the movement that carries it, even though its followers are weak while their opponents are equipped with resources (zad wa 'ttad, i.e., provisions and equipment), are powerful and tyrannical, and are inflicting oppression upon them. For at the time this surah was revealed, the Islamic movement in Makkah was passing through exactly such conditions. The stories of earlier prophets are an important material and a means of training within the educational method of the Qur'an.

Some links of the story of Musa (peace be upon him) have already passed in Surah al-Baqarah, Surah al-Ma'idah, Surah al-A'raf, Surah Yunus, Surah al-Isra, Surah al-Kahf and Surah Ta-Ha, while in some other surahs there are also brief allusions to the life of Musa (peace be upon him).

Wherever a link of this story has been alluded to, or a link has been given in detail, that link and that portion have been most fitting to the subject under discussion; in every place the appropriate portion has been brought in accordance with the context of the speech. Just as the links in this story are proportionate to the theme of this surah and clarify the same purpose. (For details see Fi Zilal, Para Six.)

The section given here relates to prophethood and its denial. The events of denial, and of the plot against Musa and his companions, leading to the drowning of Pharaoh and his people are presented, and it is explained that Musa and his companions were delivered from the clutches of the oppressors. Thus this entire link is a confirmation of the verse:

﴿وَسَيَعْلَمُ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا أَيَّ مُنقَلَبٍ يَنقَلِبُونَ﴾ (26:227) "And those who have done wrong will soon know what final return they will be returned to." It is also a confirmation of Allah's saying:

﴿فَقَدْ كَذَّبُوا فَسَيَأْتِيهِمْ أَنبَاءُ مَا كَانُوا بِهِ يَسْتَهْزِئُونَ﴾ (26:6) "So they have denied, and the news of what they used to mock will soon reach them."

This portion of the story of Musa consists of several scenes which needed to be shown. Between these scenes there are gaps and intervals in which the curtain on the scene falls, and when it rises again, the next scene is before the eyes. This is the feature that has been preserved throughout the Qur'an when presenting stories.

In this link there are seven scenes. In the first scene, a call comes from Allah. Musa converses with his Lord, is honoured with the office of prophethood, and revelation comes to him. In the second scene, Kalim (the Interlocutor) and Pharaoh come face to face. Pharaoh's courtiers are also present there. Musa presents the message, and the miracles of the staff and the luminous hand are shown. In the third scene, the magicians are brought against Musa. People gather in a vast field and there is discussion of the opponent's plans. In the fourth scene, the magicians are gathered in Pharaoh's court and are receiving firm promises of reward and honour if they win the field. The fifth scene is the scene of the contest: the contest takes place, the magicians believe, and Pharaoh threatens them. In the sixth scene there are glimpses of both camps: on one side is the scene of divine revelation, where Musa is commanded by Allah to prepare and to leave by night with My servants; on the other side Pharaoh sends his agents to all the regions and armies are assembled. In the seventh scene, the pursuing army and the fleeing believers stand before a sea. The sea splits, and through those watery paths the oppressed pass across while the oppressors are drowned.

These same scenes are presented in Surah al-A'raf, Surah Yunus and Surah Ta-Ha as well. But in each place the manner and colouring of the story differ, and the story is brought in the manner of the direction in which the discourse is heading. Thus the aspect of the story that is related to the subject under discussion is highlighted.

In Surah al-A'raf the story begins directly with a brief dialogue between Kalim and Pharaoh. Then a glimpse of the contest with the magicians is shown, while the plots and intrigues of Pharaoh and his chiefs are shown well and in detail, and between the contest with the magicians and the drowning of Pharaoh's army, Musa is brought on the scene showing miracles in Egypt. Then, when this army passes safely through the sea, several phases of life of migration are presented. Here in this surah, however, these links have been omitted, and the dialogue between Musa and Pharaoh on the subject of tawhid is given at length, because this is the theme of this surah, and this very dialogue is at its height between the polytheists of Makkah and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In Surah Yunus the story begins with a brief dialogue between Kalim and Pharaoh, the miracles of the staff and the luminous hand are not shown, and the details of the dialogue with the magicians are also omitted; whereas here both are brought in detail. In Ta-Ha, the intimate conversation between Musa and the Lord the Exalted is brought in detail. Then the encounter of Musa and Pharaoh and the contest with the magicians are cursory, while the migration journey of the Children of Israel is detailed. Here the scenes of the story end with the drowning of Pharaoh.

Thus, when we find this story repeatedly in various surahs of the Qur'an, the artistry of the Qur'anic style appears before us: nowhere do we see that it is the same story being repeated, because in each place different links are shown, different scenes are presented, one particular aspect of the story is opened up and explained, and the manner of expression is new each time. All these features make the story new in every place, and in every place the story is also in harmony with its subject.

Their case is strange and astonishing, and so is the case of every such people who exceed all limits.

The case of Pharaoh and his people was not new to Musa (peace be upon him); he knew them well. He was well aware of Pharaoh's oppression, his tyranny and his arrogance, and knew well that this was a great and difficult mission entrusted to him.

For this reason, he places his weaknesses before his Lord. Not because he wished to shrink from this call or to make a permanent excuse, but because he sought the further necessary help and support for this mission.

﴿قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي أَخَافُ أَن يُكَذِّبُونِ * وَيَضِيقُ صَدْرِي وَلَا يَنطَلِقُ لِسَانِي فَأَرْسِلْ إِلَىٰ هَارُونَ * وَلَهُمْ عَلَيَّ ذَنبٌ فَأَخَافُ أَن يَقْتُلُونِ﴾ (26:12-14) He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me. My chest will be constricted and my tongue will not be loosed, so send to Harun. And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me."

Here the words of Musa (peace be upon him) that are quoted apparently show that he speaks these words merely out of fear of denial, but he is being given prophethood in circumstances where there is a tightness in his heart and he does not have fluency of speech. In the matter of prophethood he will have to debate and converse with everyone, and his condition is that there is a stammer in his tongue, and he has stated this explicitly in Surah Ta-Ha:

﴿وَاحْلُلْ عُقْدَةً مِّن لِّسَانِي * يَفْقَهُوا قَوْلِي﴾ (20:27-28) "And loosen a knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech."

When a person has a stammer in his tongue, a tightness arises in his chest because of it. This tightness is extremely painful when a person wants to speak and wants to express arguments along with his feelings, and the tongue abandons him at that very moment. As the flood of thoughts and emotions surges, the tongue shuts and the heart constricts, and the person's condition becomes pitiable to see. Everyone has seen this state. Therefore Musa (peace be upon him) is anxious that if in such circumstances his tongue were to be tied up, it would be a very strange position, especially when the confrontation is with a tyrant and oppressor like Pharaoh. So he placed his weakness before his Lord, and at the same time made the request that Harun be also granted the station of prophethood, that he be made a partner in this office, so that both of them together might perform this great duty. The purpose was not that Musa (peace be upon him) was hesitating to accept this office or wished to shirk it. Harun, being more eloquent than Musa and calmer of heart and mind emotionally, would, if during speech Musa's tongue were tied, be present and carry the argument and dialogue forward. Musa (peace be upon him) also made a special supplication to remove this stammer, as in Surah Ta-Ha, and it is possible that Allah removed it; yet he still prayed that Harun be made a partner in the office, and said that he be appointed as his minister.

Thus he said:

﴿وَلَهُمْ عَلَيَّ ذَنبٌ فَأَخَافُ أَن يَقْتُلُونِ﴾ (26:14) "And they have a charge against me, so I fear that they will kill me." Therefore Musa (peace be upon him) was not afraid of confronting Pharaoh, nor did he seek to avoid the performance of his duty; rather he wished to have Harun appointed as minister and co-worker, so that if these people put him to death for the crime of killing, then after him the work of prophethood would be continued by Harun, and in this way the duty of prophethood would go on being performed as Allah had commanded.

Thus Musa (peace be upon him) adopted these precautionary measures for the sake of the Islamic call and prophethood. He was not particularly concerned for the person of the preacher. That is, if Musa's tongue were tied and he could not deliver a speech, Harun would be ready; it should not be that the newly arrived prophet is speaking before the people and suddenly his speech stops, and in this way the call of Islam would face a weakness. Likewise, if he were simply killed, the work of the call would come to a halt, whereas it is essential that the work of the call continue. Musa's (peace be upon him) thinking was entirely natural, because Allah had chosen him precisely for this work, had trained him under His own supervision for this very purpose, and had made him for His own work.

When Musa expressed this concern, and voiced his apprehensions and precautionary measures regarding the call, Allah accepted his request and gave him reassurance that he should not fear. The stage of the acceptance of the prayer here is extremely brief. The making of Harun a prophet, Musa's arrival in Egypt, and his meeting with Harun have been omitted, and only this is shown: Musa and Harun, both carrying the commands of their Lord, are preparing to converse with Pharaoh. But Musa's apprehensions are checked with only one strong word, which carries the sense of "no" and is meant as a warning:

Therefore Allah sent Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) again, so that they might correct their beliefs, rescue them from Pharaoh's servitude, and, after giving them good training, re-establish them upon the belief in Tawhid.

……

Up to this point we see that Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) were granted prophethood, revelation was sent to them, and they were given the mission of the Islamic call. Now the curtain falls, and in the second scene we are again standing in Pharaoh's court. Between these two scenes, the unnecessary actions and movements are cut out, and this is a particular style of Qur'anic expression: it cuts out or abbreviates the unnecessary parts between scenes and visions.

From these allusions in the story of Musa, it becomes clear that Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) were not sent as messengers to Pharaoh so that Musa would invite Pharaoh and his people to enter the religion of Islam and accept the religion of Islam. Rather, they were sent to him only so that they might make a demand upon Pharaoh and his people for the freedom of the Children of Israel. They would be liberated from his servitude, and then they might worship their Lord as they wished. They were already followers of the religion of Islam: they accepted the religion of Ya'qub and Yusuf. However, their views and their minds had deviated, and corruption had entered their beliefs. Therefore Allah sent Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) again, so that they might correct their beliefs, rescue them from Pharaoh's servitude, and, after giving them good training, re-establish them upon the belief in Tawhid.

……

Up to this point we see that Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) were granted prophethood, revelation was sent to them, and they were given the mission of the Islamic call. Now the curtain falls, and in the second scene we are again standing in Pharaoh's court. Between these two scenes, the unnecessary actions and movements are cut out, and this is a particular style of Qur'anic expression: it cuts out or abbreviates the unnecessary parts between scenes and visions.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 18–22:

Qala alam nurabbika … Bani Isra'il (22)

Pharaoh is greatly astonished. He cannot believe that Musa could make so great a claim, that he is the Messenger of the Lord of the worlds, and then make so great a demand upon Pharaoh.

"An arsil ma'anā Banī Isrā'īl" (26:18): "That you send the Children of Israel with us." Because when they had last seen Musa, he was a foster-child in their house, whose basket they had taken from the river, and then, after he killed a Copt, he had fled. That Copt was wrongfully quarrelling with an Israelite. It is related in the narrations that this Copt was among the courtiers of Pharaoh. Musa (peace be upon him) remained absent for ten years, and now he has come with this great and unimaginable demand. For this reason Pharaoh begins his speech with extreme astonishment, contempt and a mocking manner, saying: you are the very one who did these things, and now:

Qala alam … al-kafirin (26:19): "Pharaoh said: Did we not raise you among us as a child? You spent several years of your life with us, and after that you did what you did. You are truly an ungrateful man." Is this the return for the upbringing and honour that you are giving us? Now you have come and you are opposing the system of life according to which we run our order, so that you may incite rebellion against the king in whose house you were raised, and you speak of a god, lord and ruler other than me. You lived among us for a period, and at that time you never made any such plan, nor did you make claims such as you are making now. You did not warn us of this great programme.

Pharaoh also presents the incident of the killing of the Copt with great exaggeration and reminds Musa in a threatening manner.

"Wa fa'alta fa'latalaka allati fa'alta" (26:19): "And you did your deed which you did." That is, a very evil act, so evil that it is not even good to bring it out openly with clarity. You committed so great a crime.

"Wa anta min al-kafirin" (26:19): "Thus you became one who denies the Lord of the worlds." And now you speak of that very Lord of the worlds. At that time you did not speak of the Lord of the worlds.

In this way Pharaoh enumerated all the conclusive arguments in refutation of Musa (peace be upon him), and he thought that perhaps after these arguments Musa would be left speechless and unable to respond. In particular, he also pointed to an earlier homicide case, and indirectly threatened that proceedings in that case could be initiated against them and the retributive punishment (qisas) could be enforced upon them.

But the prayer of Musa had already been accepted. Now there was no knot in his tongue, and he spoke with great fluency.

Qala fa'altuha … al-mursalin (26:21), wa tilka ni'matun tamunnuha 'alayya an 'abbadta Bani Isra'il (26:22): Musa (peace be upon him) replied: "At that time I did that act unknowingly. Then I fled from you out of fear. After that my Lord gave me wisdom and included me among the messengers. As for your favour which you have reminded me of, the reality is that you had enslaved the Children of Israel." When I committed the act, I was ignorant; at that time I did this deed out of support for my oppressed people. I did not do this act in support of that outlook on life which Allah has now granted me as wisdom.

"Faraartu minkum lamma khiftukum" (26:21): "Then I fled from you when I feared you." Because I feared for my life. Allah wished for my safety; He was to grant me this wisdom.

"Wa ja'alani min al-mursalin" (26:21): "And included me among the messengers." I am not a new messenger; I am one of the company of messengers.

Now Musa answers the mockery of this man with mockery.

"Wa tilka ni'matun tamunnuha 'alayya an 'abbadta Bani Isra'il" (26:22): "This favour which you have reminded me of, its reality is that you enslaved the Children of Israel." I was raised in your house out of compulsion, because you had kept the Children of Israel as slaves. You used to kill their sons, and for this reason my mother was compelled to place me in a chest and commit me to the waves. Thus you people caught hold of the chest, and so I was raised in your house and was deprived of being raised in my parents' home. So is this the favour you boast of, and are these your kindnesses?

Now Pharaoh changes his line. Leaving this subject, he comes to the real matter, but even here he speaks in the manner of the arrogant, in the style of feigned ignorance, with a mocking and insolent tone, and insolence even against the Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 26, verse 23:

قال فرعون و ما رب العلمین (23)

May his house be ruined. He says about Allah, "What is the Lord of the worlds?" to the one by whom you have been sent as a messenger. This is a question in the manner of one who is, as it were, ignorant of the Lord of the worlds, but this is a manner of arrogance. He treats Musa's (peace be upon him) claim as a strange and wondrous claim, considers it something impossible to occur, and creates the impression that even discussing such a claim is futile.

Musa (peace be upon him) answers in such a way that the Lord of the worlds is the One whose divinity encompasses the whole of the visible universe: the Lord of the heavens and the earth and of all that is between them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verse 24:

قال رب السموت والارض وما بينهما ان كنتم موقنين (24)

This answer is a sufficient reply to the question posed in the manner of feigned ignorance. That is to say: O Pharaoh, the Lord of all the worlds is the Lord of this entire universe, both the visible and the unseen, and your kingdom and authority cannot reach as far as His kingdom and authority. Nor can your knowledge reach as far as the knowledge of God. Pharaoh's claim was only that he was the god and ruler of the Egyptian people, the sovereign of the Nile valley alone. Compared with the Lord of the Worlds, what kind of lordship is this? It is as insignificant as a particle within this vast universe.

Through this answer, Musa (peace be upon him) draws Pharaoh's attention to this great universe. He declares the lordship that Pharaoh himself claimed to be worthless and false, and invites him to open his mind by reflecting on this universe and to see the vast scope of the sovereignty of the Lord of the Worlds. Then he adds a brief remark: you can reflect only if

﴿إِن كُنتُم مُّوقِنِينَ﴾ (26:23) "if you wish to be certain." If you wish to be certain, then the Lord of the Worlds alone is worthy of certainty.

Now Pharaoh turns to his courtiers and asks them: do you not see what this gentleman is saying?

"Pharaoh said to those around him: 'Do you not listen?'"

"Do you not hear what this man is saying? These are things that no one has said in our presence, and we have never heard the like of them."

Moses (peace be upon him) did not pause but launched a second attack and further introduced the Lord of the Worlds.

Pharaoh felt this deeply, because the blow fell directly upon Pharaoh's claims and his conduct. Moses (peace be upon him) meant that the Lord of the worlds is your Lord as well as the Lord of your forefathers, and that you, O Pharaoh, are also a lowly servant among the servants of the Lord of the worlds, and that you are not the lord of anyone, despite your claim to be the lord of Egypt. Therefore your claim to divinity, lordship and sovereignty is utterly false from its very foundation. Allah is the Lord of the worlds; He was, He is, and He will remain.

This was a severely devastating bombardment upon Pharaonic ideas, and there was a fear that his courtiers too would be affected by it. Therefore he could not remain patient, and so he repeated against Moses the same accusation that the arrogant ones (mustakbirin) have always repeated.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verse 27:

قال ان رسولكم الذي ارسل اليكم لمجنون (27)

"[Pharaoh] said: Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is certainly mad." (27)

This messenger who, by his own claim, has been sent to you, appears to have a deranged mind. This man, in making these insulting remarks about the Messenger of God, does so in order that they may not have an effect on the people and that they may not come to believe him. The aim is not that Prophet Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) was actually sent at all. He says this as a mockery: that the things this man speaks are in conflict with our firmly established system, and our system has been running for centuries, according to which we are the lords, and he is calling to some other Lord of the worlds, and then he also says that this Lord of the worlds is the Lord of our forefathers as well.

But what effect will this mockery and ridicule have on Prophet Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam)? He speaks with that prophetic confidence before which the intellectual world of great tyrants is shaken like an earthquake. Therefore, he says:

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verse 28:

Qala Rabbu al-mashriqi wa al-maghribi wa ma baynahuma in kuntum ta'qilun (28)

The rising and setting of the sun are seen by people every day, and in this world they present a beautiful scene. This scene is indeed a lesson-giving one, but because it repeats itself continuously within every 24 hours, people are not affected by it at all. People have become accustomed to it. Just as the words "rising" and "setting" bring to mind the concept of the sunrise and sunset, so too the concept of the places of rising and setting is also present in them. The Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) presented these two scenes so that the phenomena of rising and setting, and the places of rising and the places of setting, cannot be changed by any tyrant. Nor can anyone deny this particular feature of these two scenes: that from the beginning of creation until today, there has been no change or advance or delay in this system. Even a dull-minded person, if he reflects upon these realities, cannot remain unaffected. Hearts that are most heedless awaken. Musa (peace be upon him), in this dialogue, is making every effort to awaken their consciences, inviting them to reflect and think.

In kuntum ta'qilun (26:28): "If you have any intellect." Tyrant rulers fear nothing in the world as much as they fear the awakening of the nation. They are very afraid of the awakening of hearts and minds. These tyrant rulers always look upon with extreme contempt those who awaken people. Therefore, such rulers always make such people the target of oppression and persecution. This is why Pharaoh becomes very angry at Musa (peace be upon him). When he sees that the call of Musa is touching the peaceful strings of hearts and minds, he then becomes agitated. He issues threats and speaks of open violence, and at the time when a person's arsenal of arguments runs out, he resorts to violence.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verse 29:

Pharaoh said: "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among those imprisoned." (26:29)

This is the argument and proof of the rebellious. The threat that you will be thrown into prison. The prison is ready, it is not far away, and it is no new thing. When tyrants become helpless, and when they sense that their position is weakening in the face of truth, because truth is always aggressive, then imprisonment becomes the last weapon of the rebellious who have no answer. This last weapon has been used from ancient times until today.

But Prophet Musa does not lose heart. After all, he is a true messenger. Allah stands with him and his brother, and He is watching. So when Pharaoh wants to end the line of argument, Musa opens its second chapter. He puts a question on a new subject, a new argument.

"Musa said: 'Even if I bring you something clear?' That is, even if I present a clear and manifest proof of my messengership, you would still punish me by sending me to prison. In this way Musa puts Pharaoh in a very difficult position before his chiefs, who were listening to this whole conversation. If Pharaoh does not listen to Musa's words, it becomes established that Pharaoh has been silenced, although he has already said that this man is a madman. So, compelled, he said: 'Very well, bring your proof.'"

' "Produce it, if you are among the truthful." 

"Bring it, if your claim is true, or if you claim that you have some miraculous proof, and if you are truthful in that claim." This person is still expressing doubt about the truth of Musa (peace be upon him). The purpose is that the people sitting around him may not be influenced.

Now Musa presents his miracles. Since the challenge and counter-challenge with Pharaoh have reached their limit, the time has come to deliver the final blow against Pharaoh.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 32–33:

﴿Then he cast down his staff, and behold, it was a serpent, plainly visible.﴾ (32)

From the manner of expression it is understood that the staff had in reality become a serpent. It came alive and began to crawl upon the ground, and when they drew out his hand from beneath his arm, it was indeed white, and this meaning is understood from the word (فاذا هي, "behold, it was"). This was not mere illusion or imagination, as sorcerers produce, where things remain upon their own reality and the disturbance lies only in the perception of people. The realities of things do not change.

The great miracle of life, which flows upon this earth, and this miracle occurs continually, does not attract people's attention, because they have become accustomed to it. This miracle is repeated again and again upon this earth, or people do not observe that transformation which takes place through life. But when Moses (peace be upon him) placed these two miracles before Pharaoh, it was a matter such that at first sight it overwhelmed the people.

Pharaoh now perceived that this miracle was, in any case, very great and possessed great power within it. Therefore he immediately resolved to confront the effects of this miracle. Within his own heart he knew well that his position was wrong. It was also possible that his courtiers, out of flattery, would not tell him the real situation. Therefore this man placed before his courtiers the danger that was coming from Moses and the people of Moses, so that he might be able to diminish the effects of these miracles.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 34–35:

[Qal lil-mala' ... tamurun (35)]

From Pharaoh's own remark it is clear that he too acknowledges this to be an extraordinary miracle, although he calls it sorcery. For he says of Moses (peace be upon him) that he is a skilled sorcerer. The evidence of his bewilderment is that the people too have been impressed by the miracle.

﴿Yuridu an yukhrijakum min ardikum bi-sihrihi﴾ (26:35) "He wants to drive you out of your land by his sorcery." This shows that Pharaoh has been defeated from within. Now he speaks to his people in a most courteous manner, although to these same people he had said, "I am your lord," and they used to prostrate before him. Now this "lord" himself consults them, saying: tell me how this matter should be resolved.

It is the pattern of all dictators in this world that they are full of pomp and arrogance, but as soon as they see that the ground is slipping from under their feet, they are compelled to speak like humble people. Then they seek refuge among the masses. Yet when they were out of danger, they used to crush these same masses. Outwardly they pretend that they seek consultation and counsel, but in reality their true nature is that of a great dictator, and they show this gentleness only to the extent that the danger is removed. But as soon as the danger passes, these people become just as tyrannical and just as oppressive as before.

The courtiers of Pharaoh advised that they (Moses and Aaron) be detained. This was because, deceived by Pharaoh's scheme, they were in a state of confusion, and they were equal partners with Pharaoh in his false system, and they also had a stake in the continuation of the Pharaonic order, since it was precisely because of this system that they were among Pharaoh's favoured nobles. Their fear was that if the common people also began to obey Moses along with the Children of Israel, these nobles might be overpowered by them. If the people had seen only these two miracles of Moses and then begun to listen to his words, the courtiers advised that they be stopped, and that a counter-sorcery be arranged against his sorcery. After preparation, a contest should take place.

قالوآ ارجہ واخاہ وابعث فی المدآئن حشیرین (36) یاتوک بکل سحار علیم (7) 3

That is: detain him and his brother, and send heralds into the great cities of Egypt, and let them bring to you every skilled and learned sorcerer, so that there may be an open contest between Musa and the sorcerers.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 38–40:

﴿فَجُمِعَ السَّحَرَةُ لِمِيقَاتِ يَوْمٍ مَّعْلُومٍ﴾ ... ﴿وَأَن كُنَّا نَحْنُ الْغَالِبِينَ﴾ (40)

From these words of Pharaoh it is apparent that he was creating tremendous enthusiasm among the people in support of the sorcerers.

﴿هَلْ أَنتُم مُّجْتَمِعُونَ﴾ (39) ﴿لَعَلَّنَا نَتَّبِعُ السَّحَرَةَ إِن كَانُوا هُمُ الْغَالِبِينَ﴾ (40)

"Will you go to the gathering? Perhaps we may follow the sorcerers if they are the victors." That is, will you certainly come on the day of the contest and not remain behind? So that we may see how the sorcerers win the field, and how the Egyptians prevail over Moses and the Children of Israel. Ordinary people always gather on such occasions, but they do not know the real truth, that rulers use the common people and make toys of them in these gatherings, assemblies and processions. And they do this so that the common people will not get the opportunity to reflect on the oppression they inflict upon them and on their backwardness for which they are responsible; let them be occupied with the contest of Moses and the sorcerers and be entertained.

Before the contest, the sorcerers appear in Pharaoh's court. They want an assurance that if they succeed, they will be given a suitable reward. They obtain a firm promise from Pharaoh that if they succeed, they will receive a suitable wage along with proximity to the royal throne and crown, and that they will be among his close courtiers.

Now the two armies are ready for the contest, and the people have gathered.

He said to them... "the first of the believers" (51)

Then Moses (peace be upon him) threw down his staff, and suddenly it was swallowing up what they had falsely contrived. Thereupon all the sorcerers fell down prostrate involuntarily and said, "We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron (peace be upon them)." Pharaoh said, "You have believed in him before I gave you permission! Surely he is your chief who taught you magic. Very well, you will soon come to know. I will cut off your hands and feet on opposite sides and crucify you all." They replied, "No harm; we will return to our Lord. We hope that our Lord will forgive us our sins, because we were the first of the believers."

This scene begins with great seriousness and a dignified manner. However, since Moses (peace be upon him) has truth and divine support with him, he is not at all anxious. Pharaoh has summoned the expert, cunning sorcerers of the entire land, and has also gathered a vast crowd of misguided and simple-minded common people. But Moses (peace be upon him) pays no heed at all to these official preparations. Moses's composure is expressed in the fact that he gives the sorcerers the opportunity to display their feats first.

"Moses said to them: Throw what you are going to throw" (26:43). Moses's manner of expression is such that he does not attach importance to their feats. "Throw what you are going to throw."

"Throw what you are going to throw" (26:43). You say this with indifference and without any special arrangement. Accordingly, the sorcerers brought forth their entire resources, their complete skill and their complete cunning, invoked the name of Pharaoh, and began their turn.

"So they threw down their ropes and their staffs, and said, 'By the might of Pharaoh, we will surely be the victors'" (26:44).

"They immediately threw down their ropes and staffs and said, 'By the glory of Pharaoh, we shall certainly prevail.'" The details of their ropes and staffs are not given here in this context; details are given in Surah al-A'raf and Surah Ta-Ha. This is because the context here seeks to maintain Moses's deep composure. Here the full action of Moses is shown immediately, because the triumph of truth is the axis and theme of this surah.

"Then Moses threw down his staff, and suddenly it was swallowing up what they had falsely contrived" (26:45). An event occurred whose like they could not have imagined. They had exhausted their final artistic abilities. They had spent their whole lives in this trickery and had attained complete mastery in it. They had presented every feat that a sorcerer can perform. They had come in large numbers, group after group, from every direction. Moses (peace be upon him) was alone, with only his staff. This staff swallowed up all their ropes and staffs. (Alif) The lexical meaning is to gulp down, that is, to devour something very quickly. The sorcerers well knew that by sorcery a staff cannot swallow up anything. Sorcery involves only imagination and hypnotic illusion, but the staff in reality swallowed all the thrown objects. Not a trace of anything remained on the field. Had it been sorcery, then after the effect of sorcery and the end of the illusion, the objects should have remained present. When they saw that in the field, in practice, nothing was left... they became certain that Moses was by no means a sorcerer. He is a prophet of the truth, and the best knowers of this truth in this world were these very sorcerers.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 46–48:

﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrate.﴾ (26:46) "They said: We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron." (26:47–48)

Only a moment earlier they were hired people, bargaining with Pharaoh over their skill and their wages. They held no creed and had no lofty aim before them. But now the truth that reached their hearts transformed them completely. That event shook them to the core. An earthquake occurred in their religious world, and the truth they saw with their own eyes penetrated to the depths of their hearts. It removed every veil from their hearts, and the layers of error that had settled upon their hearts were cleared away. For they knew that if Moses were merely a sorcerer, their ropes and staffs would not have vanished; his sorcery could create agitation in those objects, but they could not disappear.

So their hearts became clear, and they had no recourse but to fall down in prostration without intending to do so, to declare their faith, and to adopt it openly and plainly.

﴿We believe in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron.﴾ (26:47–48) "We have come to believe in the Lord of the worlds, who is the Lord of Moses and Aaron."

The human heart is a wondrous thing. In a single moment its world can change; in one glance a revolution can take place within it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke most truly: "The heart of every person is between two fingers of the Most Merciful; if Allah wills, He keeps it upright, and if He wills, He causes it to go astray (crooked)." Thus the sorcerers, who had been seekers of reward and hired people, became noble believers, and they stood upright before Pharaoh and his tyrannical, oppressive companions. They paid no regard even to the crowd of common people that Pharaoh had gathered. They embraced Islam without caring for the consequences that they could expect from the oppressive, tyrannical Pharaoh. They understood well what it meant to believe in Moses in opposition to Pharaoh, and to declare it openly in this manner. Now, in their eyes, it held no importance what anyone might say.

The sudden turn of events was, of course, a thunderbolt upon Pharaoh and his chieftains, since the people had all gathered. They had been gathered by Pharaoh himself and his officials so that they might watch the contest between Moses and the sorcerers. They had spread propaganda among the populace that Moses the Israelite had brought a great sorcery and intended, by means of magic, to overthrow our government and establish the rule of his own people. The government had assembled great sorcerers to counter him; our sorcerers would prevail over him and eliminate him. The people gathered and saw that Moses came invoking the name of Allah. Immediately the sorcerers acknowledged the prophethood of Moses, that he was a true prophet from Allah. They declared that we acknowledge the Lord of Moses and Aaron. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verse 49:

Qal amantum... ajma'in (26:39): "Did you believe in him without my permission and without consulting me? You submitted to Moses and prostrated yourselves at his word." Here he did not say amantum bihi ("you believed in him"), but said amantum lahu, that is, you bowed your heads before him in submission. Without my permission, just as a person who lays a military stratagem is master of his own resolve, knows his target, and estimates its outcome. A person who does everything through planning cannot understand that moment of grace and that natural touch by which the hearts of the sorcerers were seized. Tyrannical rulers cannot grasp such moments, because their hearts become stone and they are deprived of such luminous moments. Therefore Pharaoh hastily levels accusations against them and gives the common people a line that the sorcerers' hearts were so greatly transformed for what reason.

Innahu lakabirukum alladhi 'allamakumu as-sihr (26:39): "Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic." Pharaoh made this strange accusation. What connection could Moses (peace be upon him) have with the sorcerers, unless it was that when these sorcerers were soothsayers and Moses (peace be upon him) was being raised in Pharaoh's house, the soothsayers perhaps taught Moses (peace be upon him) at that time, or Moses (peace be upon him) used to go to their places of worship. On the basis of this connection he made this accusation. Then, instead of telling them that Moses is your student, he levelled the accusation that he is your great teacher. He wants to prove to the common people that Moses (peace be upon him) is a threat to the country.

After this he openly threatens them with severe punishment, saying: well, wait for my punishment.

Falasawfa ta'lamun... ajma'in (26:39): "Very well, you will soon know. I will have your hands and feet cut off from opposite sides and crucify you all." This is the folly that every tyrant dictator commits, and he commits it at the time when his chair and power are threatened and his own person is threatened, and in it he does not even care for the reproach of his own conscience. And it is clear that Pharaoh is announcing this punishment, whose word is law and is enforced immediately. Now let us also hear the words of the believing group who have seen the light.

This is the word of a heart which has attained the recognition of Allah, and after that recognition it has no concern about what may be lost. This is the word of a heart which has reached Allah and tasted the sweetness of faith. Therefore it pays no heed to the dictator and the tyrannical ruler, and this is the cry of a heart that seeks the Hereafter, and so it no longer cares for the benefit of this world, whether little or much.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 50–51:

"Qalu la darar" ... "al-mu'minin" (26:51). "No harm!" We no longer have any concern about having our hands and feet cut off. We feel no worry about torture or the punishment of the cross. We do not fear death or martyrdom. We care nothing for these things. If we die, we will go to our Lord. After all, what is there for us in the life of this earth? Our aim now is this:

"Inna yaghfir lana rabbuna khatayana" (26:51), "that our Lord forgive us our sins," and that He forgive these sins because of the honour of this, that

"Inna kunna awwal al-mu'minin" (26:51), "we became the first to believe." Now we hold the rank of the foremost of the believers (al-sabiqun al-awwalun).

O Allah! How glorious is faith when it illuminates the world of the conscience. When its effusion falls upon the soul. When the bowl of the believer's heart is filled with faith, this earthly body ascends to the station of 'Illiyyun. The heart becomes rich. Within hearts the wealth of faith is gathered, and in comparison with it, all the wealth of the earth's surface appears worthless.

Now, within the context of the discourse, the curtain falls once again, and this scene of the sorcerers' illuminated conscience disappears from view. No further comment is made on it, so that the profound effect of these foremost believers remains alive in the reader's heart. People should reflect that what the people of Makkah are inflicting upon the believers is nothing new. In history, believers have endured such kinds of oppression again and again.

Now a scene of Pharaoh's schemes against the believers, and a scene of Allah's guidance for the believers:

Verses 52–56 (Wa-awhayna ilá … hadhirun): Here there is a large and long gap in events and time. A long span of time and a number of events are omitted from the middle. After this contest, Hadrat Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) also continued working in Egypt, and the other miracles mentioned in Surah al-A'raf also occurred during this period. Finally the time came when Allah the Exalted commanded Hadrat Musa (peace be upon him) to take the Children of Israel and leave Egypt. However, in this Surah all those events are wrapped up and left aside, and only those parts of the story of Musa are taken here which are related to the theme and subject matter of this Surah.

Allah the Exalted gave Hadrat Musa permission through revelation that he should take his people and leave Egypt. All the Children of Israel were to leave at night. Very organized and secret arrangements were made for this journey, and Hadrat Musa (peace be upon him) was also informed that Pharaoh would pursue them at all costs, and that they should set out towards the seashore. It appears that Hadrat Musa reached the seashore at this place, which was in the present-day area of the Gulf of Suez and the small lakes; this is where it took place.

Pharaoh received secret reports that the Children of Israel were about to leave. So he too ordered his people that as soon as the exodus began, the armies should be kept ready to pursue them. He sent his messengers to all regions to prepare the armies, saying that this is a small group; they are thinking of ways to escape. But he did not know that this exodus was being organized by Allah the Exalted.

Pharaoh's people kept preparing the armies, but how could a sense of unease not arise among the common people: what great power does Musa have that such extensive preparations are being made against him, while Pharaoh calls himself a god, and yet makes such military preparations against a single member of the public? So at this moment Pharaoh felt the need for this kind of announcement.

﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾ (26:54). So the question is: then why is such arrangement being made against them, and why are armies being gathered, if they are a small band?

﴿And indeed, they have enraged us﴾ (26:55): these people say and do things that no one has done before us, so because of them we fall into rage and a spirit of revenge has arisen within us.

Although these people are extremely dangerous and their movement is a strong movement, the government officials should tell the public that the government has taken complete precautionary measures and is keeping watch over them.

﴿And indeed, we are a people who are always on guard﴾ (26:56): and we are awake against their plots. We are taking great caution in their affairs and controlling them well. Whenever the people of falsehood confront the people of faith, the people of falsehood become bewildered and distressed in the same way in the face of the believers.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 60–66:

فاخرجنھم من ……اسرآئیل (59)

These people went out only so that they might pursue Musa and his people and seize them, but this going out of theirs from their homes was their last going out. The Children of Israel could neither cross the sea, nor did they have any equipment for war with Pharaoh, and Pharaoh was pursuing them with full equipment and had prepared a merciless plan to seize them.

Apparently the circumstances indicate that there is no way for them to escape now. Ahead is the sea, and behind them the enemy is advancing.

قَالَ أَصْحَابُ مُوسَىٰ إِنَّا لَمُدْرَكُونَ (26:61) "The companions of Musa said: 'We are surely overtaken.'" The restlessness of the believers has now reached its limit. Now it is a matter of a few minutes before the army of Pharaoh kills or captures them, and apparently there is no way to escape.

But the connection of Hazrat Musa was established with the higher world. Revelation was continuously coming to him. His heart was full of tranquility. He was fully certain that Allah would devise a way out, that a means of help would emerge, and that Allah had promised deliverance. Although he too did not know how the matter would turn out, he was certain that deliverance was assured, because this entire plan was devised by Allah.

قَالَ كَلَّا ۖ إِنَّ مَعِيَ رَبِّي سَيَهْدِينِ (26:62) "He said: 'Never! Surely my Lord is with me; He will guide me.'" The word كَلَّا is used in a place where negation is intended with strong emphasis; that is, "you will by no means be seized, and you will by no means fall into trouble; Allah will by no means let you be lost. My Lord is with me, and He will surely guide me." Hazrat Musa speaks with great emphasis, confidence and certainty. In these dark moments of despair, a ray of light suddenly appears. The path to deliverance comes from the direction from which no hope was expected.

فَأَوْحَيْنَا إِلَىٰ مُوسَىٰ أَنِ اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْبَحْرَ (26:63) "So We revealed to Musa: 'Strike the sea with your staff.'" Now in the flow of the discourse, it is not said further that they struck the sea with the staff; rather, the result is quickly placed before us.

فَانفَلَقَ فَكَانَ كُلُّ فِرْقٍ كَالطَّوْدِ الْعَظِيمِ (26:63) "Then it split, and each part became like a huge mountain." This miracle occurred, and what people called impossible came to pass, because their reasoning was based on the ordinary, everyday events, and these everyday events also take place according to the principles established by Allah's power, and they run according to those principles for as long as Allah wills. Allah's command was that the water stood up on both sides of the path like mountains. The Children of Israel crossed the river by passing through.

Pharaoh, with his armies, stood bewildered on the other side. They witnessed this miracle with their own eyes. It is certain that for some time he was left astonished, seeing that Musa and his people had gone and passed through. He must still have considered sending his armies into that path, because it was a strange action.

By this plan of Allah, the Children of Israel went out to the other side. While the water was still in two parts, Pharaoh and his army were still within the water when Allah brought their end near.

وَأَزْلَفْنَا ثَمَّ الْآخَرِينَ (26:64) to وَأَغْرَقْنَا الْآخَرِينَ (26:66) "And We brought the others near to that place. We saved Musa and all those who were with him, and We drowned the others." This miracle remained on the tongues of people for a long time; for centuries they continued to narrate it. Would more people have believed in it?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 60–66:

فاخرجنھم من ……اسرآئیل (59)

These people went out only so that they might pursue Musa and his people and seize them, but this going out of theirs from their homes was their last going out. In the plan of Allah, it was in fact their expulsion from those blessings and luxuries in which they were, an expulsion from superior comforts, places of honour, prosperity, gardens and palaces. After this they never returned to those places, and this was their punishment for the oppression they used to inflict upon the weak.

وَأَوْرَثْنَاهَا بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ (26:59) "And We made the Children of Israel inheritors of them." History does not mention that the Children of Israel re-entered Egypt after the Pharaohs and took possession of the gardens, rivers and wealth of Egypt. Therefore the exegetes say that the meaning is that the wealth and power of the world were given to them, just as they were given to the Pharaonites. The purpose is that one people was given decline and another was given ascendancy, and in that ascendancy the latter became the heir of the former. What was once in the possession of the former noble position is now in the possession of the latter.

And after the punishment affecting their worldly state, now the mention comes of their physical punishment and final end.
