Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 69–70:

Lesson No. 163: Explanation of the Verses

69 … to … 104

﴿And recite to them the story of Abraham﴾ … ﴿What is it that you worship?﴾ (70)

Present to them the story of Abraham. They think that they are the heirs of Abraham and that they follow the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him). Tell them that Abraham's own father was also an idol-worshipper, and that Abraham strongly confronted his father over the act of idol-worship. Then how did you become idol-worshippers? Abraham confronted his father and his people precisely over the issue of idol-worship and polytheism. He told his father and his people plainly that idol-worship is clear misguidance, and he spoke in a harsh tone: ﴿What are these things that you worship?﴾ (26:70 – "What is it that you worship?").

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 69–70:

Lesson No. 163: Explanation of the Verses

69 … to … 104

﴿And recite to them the story of Abraham﴾ … ﴿What is it that you worship?﴾ (70)

Present to them the story of Abraham. They think that they are the heirs of Abraham and that they follow the religion of Abraham (peace be upon him). Tell them that Abraham's own father was also an idol-worshipper, and that Abraham strongly confronted his father over the act of idol-worship. Then how did you become idol-worshippers? Abraham confronted his father and his people precisely over the issue of idol-worship and polytheism. He told his father and his people plainly that idol-worship is clear misguidance, and he spoke in a harsh tone: ﴿What are these things that you worship?﴾ (26:70 – "What is it that you worship?").

They said, "We worship idols, and we remain devoted to them."

These people used to call their idols "god," yet the Qur'an, quoting their own words, also records for them the word aṣnām (idols), from which it is known that they accepted that these idols were fashioned from stone. Nevertheless, these people remained engaged in worshipping and revering these idols. This was a common weakness of their beliefs. But when beliefs and thoughts become corrupted, those who have embraced these corrupted beliefs cannot understand how this attitude is dragging them down to such depths of humiliation and degradation.

Hazrat Ibrahim (peace be upon him) awakens their heedless hearts and appeals to their intellect: do you not see how far you have fallen, and what follies you have embraced to your breast, without any thought or understanding?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 72–73:

He said: "Do they hear you when you call upon them, or do they benefit you or harm you?" (26:72–73)

The least quality that a deity must have is that it hears and responds to questions. At the very least, a god should be like the servant who worships it and humbles himself before it. These deities neither hear, nor speak, nor are they able to bring any benefit or harm. If they cannot even hear, being deaf, how will they bring benefit or harm? Therefore, it is not permissible to call upon them in any way.

None of the people gave an answer to any of Ibrahim (peace be upon him)'s questions, although they knew that Ibrahim was mocking them severely and criticising their idols and their way, because they had no answer to them. Their response was only that which every person gives who criticises without thinking and understanding.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 26, verse 74:

They said, "Nay, we found our fathers doing thus."

Surely these things neither benefit nor harm, and they do not hear; rather, our forefathers have been following this practice, so we worship these idols.

This is indeed a most shameful answer, yet the polytheists give it with great brazenness. Likewise the polytheists of Makkah also used to say this, and they felt no shame at all. Rather, for them the deed of their forefathers was itself sufficient proof, and there was no need for any further discussion. This worship of forefathers was a major obstacle in the path of Islam, because it required them to abandon the religion of their fathers, and so to abandon the following of their forefathers and, indirectly, to acknowledge that their fathers had been upon misguidance. Therefore it is not proper to claim this about the forefathers who have passed away. Thus this reverence for forefathers, a reverence without reality, has always been a major obstacle in the way of accepting the truth. Especially when people become rigid and empty in their intellect, and to free people from such stagnation, superstition and worship of forefathers, it becomes necessary to give them a great mental jolt, so that people may use free reflection and thought.

To awaken people who are drowned in this stagnation and heedlessness, it was necessary that Ibrahim (peace be upon him) give them a sharp jolt, although Ibrahim (peace be upon him) was, by his nature, extremely gentle and serious. So he proclaims: "Very well, then, I am an enemy to them, and an enemy to all those ideas which have been raised upon the foundation of this worship of idols."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 75–77:

[Qur'anic text omitted from the Urdu source]

Thus he declared that my father and my people also worship them, but I not only renounce these beliefs, I am their enemy. I am the enemy of these idols, the enemy of ancestor worship, and the enemy of the ancient history and the most ancient forefathers.

Thus the Noble Qur'an teaches the believers that when faith stands against truth, whether a father, a people, or the traditions of forefathers come forward, all of them must be rejected, because after Islam it is obligatory to sever all human ties and to adopt only the Islamic bond and relationship. In Islam, faith and ideology hold primacy, and all other things are subordinate to them.

Ibrahim (peace be upon him), while rejecting the traditions of his forefathers, makes an exception only for the traditions of the Lord of the worlds.

﴿Fa-innahum 'aduwwun li illa Rabb al-'alamin﴾ (26:77) "They are all my enemies, except the Lord of the worlds." Because among their forefathers there must certainly have been people who worshipped Allah alone, in that period of history when their beliefs had not yet been corrupted, and there must also have been some who associated the service of others with the Lord of the worlds. Therefore, showing extreme caution, he made an exception for the Lord of the worlds here, and this was fitting for a serious person like Ibrahim (peace be upon him), since he was dealing with faith, belief and ideology, and it is evident that matters of faith, belief and ideology are very delicate.

After this, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) introduces the Lord of the worlds by describing His attributes, with Whom his connection is present in every state and at every time. He is near to us. In every movement and every stillness of a human being, He is with the human being. He provides for all the needs and necessities of a human being.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 78–82:

﴿Alladhi khalaqani fahuwa yahdin﴾ (26:88)... ﴿Yawm al-Din﴾ (82)

In praising his Lord here, Ibrahim (peace be upon him) goes into the details and paints a picture of them. From this we perceive that he was immersed in the recognition of his Lord with his whole personality, and that his entire being was connected with God. He turned towards Allah with great love, and he praised his Lord as though he were seeing Allah, and with all his feelings, all his consciousness and intuition, and with all his limbs, he was finding Allah's grace and bounty. The way the Qur'an has described the relationship between Ibrahim and the Lord of the worlds, with such a gentle melody, clearly shows the atmosphere of that relationship, its traces and its reflection: a sweet and soft melody, with long and wide effects.

﴿Alladhi khalaqani fahuwa yahdin﴾ (26:78): "He who created me, and it is He who guides me." He created me, and He alone knows, while I do not know from where the parts of my body were gathered. Only He is aware of my nature and my formation. Only He is aware of the subtleties of my duties and my consciousness. Only He is aware of my wealth and my ... and He alone is fully informed. ﴿Fahuwa yahdin﴾: "It is He who guides me": He points out to me the path on which I must walk, and the system according to which I must spend my life. Ibrahim (peace be upon him) conveys the sense that he is like molten matter which the craftsman shapes as he wishes, producing products in whatever form he chooses. This is complete obedience, complete surrender, complete contentment, comfort, tranquility and trust in the Divine Being.

﴿Wa alladhi huwa yut'imuni wa yasqin﴾ (26:79) and ﴿Wa idha maridtu fahuwa yashfin﴾ (26:80): "He who feeds me and gives me drink, and when I am ill, it is He who heals me." This is direct sustenance, deep compassion, and a love that stays close. Only Ibrahim can truly feel this. In health and in sickness, in residence and in travel, in every state, he remains with the lofty manners of prophethood. He knows that sickness too comes by the will of Allah. Yet he does not attribute it to Allah, although both sickness and healing are from Allah. But in ﴿Idha maridtu fahuwa yashfin﴾ a profound respect is preserved. In the station of bounty, ﴿yut'imuni wa yasqin﴾ and ﴿yashfin﴾, he attributes these to Allah, while in trial he attributes the affliction to himself. This is the station of Ibrahim.

﴿Wa alladhi yumituni thumma yuhyin﴾ (26:81): "He who will cause me to die and then give me life again." It is the belief of every Muslim that the decision of death is made by Allah, and that one day Allah will raise him again for reckoning and accountability. Therefore, this is an expression of complete submission and contentment.

﴿Wa alladhi atma'u an yaghfira li khati'ati yawm al-Din﴾ (26:82): "And He from whom I hope that He will forgive my sin on the Day of Judgment." Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who is a prophet and messenger, has as his highest desire that Allah forgive his sins on the Day of Resurrection, although he is fully one who knows Allah. He has a deep awareness of the Being of Allah, and the recognition of his Lord is deeply woven into the depths of his soul. He does not consider his self to be pure and clean. Despite this recognition and nearness, he still fears that some fault may have occurred from him. He does not rely on his deeds, nor does he call himself deserving of salvation on the basis of his deeds. He relies on the grace of his Lord, seeks the mercy of Allah, and it is this Divine mercy that he hopes for, that there will be pardon and forgiveness, and then his salvation will come.

This is the prophetic consciousness of piety and fear of God, a consciousness based on reverence and respect, and a manner of utmost caution. This is the true consciousness of the greatness of Allah and of Allah's blessings. According to this consciousness, the value of deeds is very small, and the value of forgiveness is great.

Thus, here Ibrahim (peace be upon him) states the fundamental elements of his beliefs about the Divine Being: that the Lord of the worlds is one without partner; that even in the small affairs of human life on earth, Allah, the Lord of the worlds, exercises control; and that in resurrection after death and in reckoning, only the grace of Allah can save the servant. In terms of deeds, the servant is only deficient, and these are the matters which the polytheists and the people of Ibrahim deny.

Ibrahim (peace be upon him), who is extremely gentle of disposition and one who weeps and supplicates before Allah, advances his prayer with the utmost humility and submission, [ibrahim jo nihayat hi halim al-tabe aur Allah ke samne gira-o-buka karne wale hain wo nihayat hi khuzu-o-khushu ke sath apni dua ko aage barhate hain.]

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 83–89:

Rabbi hab ... saleem (89)

Consider this prayer of Ibrahim (peace be upon him): in it there is not a single worldly aim. He does not even say, "O Allah, grant me good health." This entire prayer is an inspiration of lofty aims and of exalted and pure consciousness. It is the prayer of a heart that has reached Allah, a heart that has nothing before it but Allah. In its sight everything other than Allah is held in contempt, and it seeks more of the stage of recognition (ma'rifah) to which it has risen. A prayer that issues from such a heart is in a state of both awe and hope, because it has seen the bounties of Allah and hopes for more.

Rabbi hab li hukman (26:83): "My Lord, bestow upon me wisdom (hukm)." O Allah, grant me such wisdom by whose light I may distinguish between the genuine and the counterfeit values, so that I remain steadfast upon a course of conduct that brings me to the enduring values.

Wa alhiqni bil-salihin (26:83): "And join me with the righteous." This is the prayer of Ibrahim, who is a prophet and a messenger, humble and gentle in disposition, and most forbearing. The humility of this exalted patriarch, the father of the prophets, is worth beholding. His caution is worth noting. How much fear of Allah there is in his words, and how much acknowledgment of his own need! He is always fearful that the human heart may at any moment incline toward evil; therefore he seeks the company and environment of the righteous, and he desires to perform righteous deeds by the grace of Allah, or to remain steadfast upon righteous conduct.

Waj'al li lisana sidqin fil-akhirin (26:83): "And grant me a true reputation among those who come after." His prayer is that the call to monotheism which he began should endure until the Day of Resurrection. He does not pray for abundance of offspring; rather, his prayer is for those who will come in future generations, following in his footsteps and admiring him, that they should accept his call to monotheism, adopt the "hanif" religion, and so on. He made this same prayer in other places in the Qur'an too, at the time when he and his son Isma'il were raising the foundations of the Ka'bah.

Rabbana waj'alna ... al-Hakim (129) (2:128-129): "Our Lord, make us both Muslims [submissive] to You, and from our progeny raise up a community that is Muslim to You; show us our rites of worship and forgive our shortcomings. Indeed You are the Oft-Forgiving, the Most Merciful. And our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from among themselves, who will recite to them Your verses, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify their lives. Indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise." Allah accepted this prayer of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). He spread his call, and in subsequent ages all people spoke well of him; and then, in accordance with his prayer, the Last Prophet appeared, and this prayer was fulfilled after thousands of years. In the reckoning of people, thousands of years of this world are very long, but with Allah they have no weight, and the wisdom of Allah required that the prayer of Ibrahim be answered after this long period.

Waj'alni min warathati jannatin-na'im (26:85): "And make me among the inheritors of the Garden of Bliss." Earlier he had prayed that he be included among the company of the righteous and be granted the ability to perform righteous deeds, so that he might walk in the ranks of the righteous and then enter that Garden whose inheritance is the right of the righteous servants.

Waghfir li abi innahu kana minad-dallin (26:86): "And forgive my father; indeed he is among those who went astray." Although his father had harshly rebuked Ibrahim and spoken threateningly to him, Ibrahim had nevertheless promised, even during that conversation, that he would keep praying for him. It is because of this promise that he is praying for his father. Later the Qur'an made clear that it is not permissible to seek forgiveness for polytheists, even if they are close relatives, and the Qur'an also explained that Ibrahim sought forgiveness for his father only because he had made a promise to him.

Falamma tabayyana lahu annahu 'aduwwul-lillahi tabarra'a minhu: "When it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him." Ibrahim understood that, in this path, "so-and-so son of so-and-so" counts for nothing; here the bond is one of ideological brotherhood. A fundamental element of Islamic upbringing is that the first bond and relationship in an Islamic society is an ideological one, and the only firm tie between one person and another can be one of ideas. When this tie is severed, all other ties are severed, and then a person becomes distant from others; no connection or relationship remains.

Wa la tukhzini yawma yub'athun (26:87), yawma la yanfa'u malun wa la banun (26:88), illa man ata Allaha biqalbin salim (26:89): "And do not disgrace me on the day they are raised up, the day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart." From this statement of Ibrahim it becomes clear how terrifying the Day of Resurrection will be, how greatly Ibrahim feared Allah, and how greatly he dreaded being humiliated before Allah. This fear arises from his own shortcomings, though he is an honoured prophet. Moreover, from this prayer, "the day when neither wealth nor children will benefit, except one who comes to Allah with a sound heart," it becomes clear how thoroughly Ibrahim (peace be upon him) understood the responsibilities of the Day of Resurrection. He also clearly understood worldly values and Islamic values. For on the Day of Resurrection only one who comes with sincerity, whose heart is devoted to Allah, and who has no idol or purpose of the world within him, will succeed. He must be free of every disease, free of every interest, free of every kind of desire and deviation, and have no connection with any deity or object of worship other than Allah. This is the soundness of heart whose weight in Islam and in the Resurrection will be significant.

Yawma la yanfa'u malun wa la banun (26:88): "The day when neither wealth nor children will benefit." On that day no worldly value or preference will be of any use, although in this world people run like dogs after such aims and preferences; yet in the scale of the Hereafter these preferences have no weight.

Now there comes one of the scenes of the Resurrection. Behold, the day which Ibrahim feared so greatly has appeared. Ibrahim is still with his hands raised and is still engaged in prayer, when upon the scene the picture of that day appears.

**Lesson No. 164: Brief Overview**

Just as in the previous story the course of time was reversed, and the discourse moved back from the story of Musa to the story of Ibrahim, here too we move further back from the story of Ibrahim to the story of Nuh (Noah, peace be upon him). The historical order of the stories is not being observed here. The purpose is to give a few examples of struggle against polytheistic beliefs.

The story of Nuh (peace be upon him) also appears in several surahs, as the stories of Musa and Ibrahim do. It appeared earlier in Surah al-A'raf. In Surah al-A'raf, after the descent of Adam, it came in brief, in which he called his people to monotheism and warned them of the great punishment of the Day of Judgment. It also told that the people of Nuh said to him that he had gone astray. They were surprised that Allah could send a man like themselves to them, to guide other people. For this reason Allah drowned his people and saved him and his companions.

This story is also presented briefly in Surah Yunus. This was the last phase of his prophetic mission, when he challenged his people. They denied him. He and his companions were saved by the ark, and the rest of the party was drowned.

The details of this story are given in Surah Hud: the ark, the flood, the prayer of Nuh concerning his son who drowned, the events after the flood, and the events that befell him during preaching before the flood.

The story also appears in Surah al-Mu'minun. There Nuh (peace be upon him) calls his people to the worship of the One Lord, while the people object that "you are only a human like us, and you say these things in order to gain superiority over us. If Allah had wished to send a prophet, He could have sent angels." They accused him of being possessed. There Nuh again turns to his Lord and seeks help, and there again there is a passing reference to the ark and the flood.

Generally, the story of Nuh comes together with the stories of 'Ad, Thamud, Lut and the people of Madyan. The same is the case in this surah. What is said in this story here is that he tells his people to fear Allah, that he seeks no reward from them, and that the leaders of his people demanded of him that he drive away the poor believers who had gathered around him. Nuh refused this, and exactly the same demand was made of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by the people of Makkah. After this, Nuh prays: "O Allah, decide between me and my people with truth." Allah fulfils this request, destroys the deniers and saves the believers.

**Lesson No. 164: Explanation of the Verses**

**Verses 105 to 122**

﴿The people of Nuh denied the messengers.﴾ (105)

Here the end of the story has been stated first; after this the details are given, so that the listener knows where the discourse is directed.

The question is: the people of Nuh denied only Nuh (peace be upon him), yet the Qur'an says that they denied the messengers. Prophethood, in its reality, is in fact one truth. The call of all messengers has been the same: that Allah is One, without partner, and that only He should be worshipped. Whoever, whether a person or a people, denies one messenger, in fact denies all the messengers. The Qur'an repeats this meaning and this reality in various places, and it is repeated in various styles and modes of expression. This is because it is an established principle of the Islamic outlook on life, and this principle is accepted in the call of all messengers. According to this principle, humanity has always been divided: those who accept the messengers on one side and those who reject them on the other. This has happened in all prophethoods and in all ages. When a Muslim looks at history, he sees that in every religion and every creed the community has always been one. From the earliest history up to today, and up to the final religion, the monotheism of Islam, in every nation and every religion the opposing party has been that of the disbelievers and the deniers. The believers are those who believe in the messengers, and the disbelievers are those who deny. The believers respect all the messengers and believe in them, because the nature and reality of the office of prophethood is one.

According to a Muslim's understanding, humanity cannot be divided according to colours, regions and races. Humanity is divided only between two groups, the people of truth (ahl-e-haqq) and the people of falsehood (ahl-e-batil), and since the beginning of humanity this has been the division. Therefore, from the Islamic point of view there is one standard and one measure for history. For this reason the mentality and thinking of a Muslim is that he thinks above colour, race, nation and homeland. His present relations or historical relations are only those that are based on the values of faith. He judges everyone by the principles of those values, and he weighs all his values and ideas by the standard of faith alone.

﴿When their brother Nuh said to them: ...obey me.﴾ (106–108)

This was the people of Nuh, who denied Nuh (peace be upon him). Their own people denied him, and he was their own brother. Whereas the demand of brotherhood was that these people should show forbearance towards Nuh and, with composure, believe and affirm him. But his own people did not even show fraternal forbearance, and the sympathetic words of their own brother had no effect upon them.

﴿Will you not fear (Allah)?﴾ (26:106). Do they not fear the consequence that necessarily follows from the attitude they hold? Their hearts do not feel fear and awe. Calling people to the fear of Allah is the specific theme of this surah. The same thing was said by Musa to Fir'aun, the same was said by Nuh to his people, and the same was said by every messenger to his own people.

﴿Indeed I am a trustworthy messenger to you.﴾ (26:108). I am a messenger who neither betrays, nor deceives, nor conceals anything, nor diminishes anything, nor exaggerates. I convey only what Allah has commanded.

﴿So fear Allah and obey me.﴾ (26:108). In this way Nuh (peace be upon him) calls them to the fear of Allah, and here he attributes the fear to Allah, and thus he encourages them to obedience and submission.

Then Nuh (peace be upon him) reassures them that his call is free of worldly aims. He tells them that his objectives are not tied to the movement of calling to Allah. ﴿Do you build on every high place a landmark for no purpose?﴾ (79)

*Rabi'* (ربع) in Arabic means high ground. It appears that they built their dwellings on elevated sites, so that from a distance the buildings looked like great mountains. Their purpose in this was to show that they were highly skilled and highly capable. This is why Allah used the word *'abath* (عبث, pointless) for it. Had they built these great landmarks to guide travellers or ships at sea, the Qur'an would not have used the word *'abath* for them. The implication is that strength, skill and wealth should be spent on beneficial purposes, not merely on display, ostentation and the demonstration of one's excellence.

Then Allah uses a meaningful phrase in this same remark:

﴿And you take for yourselves fortresses, perhaps you will live forever.﴾ (26:129) The people of ʿAd had progressed to a notable degree in civilisation and culture. For building great palaces and cutting through mountains, they had developed advanced technology. They built great towers on high places. It seemed as though they built these great palaces, lofty landmarks and towers because they believed they would live forever in this world, that the natural conditions of this world would have no effect on them, and that no enemy would ever be able to overcome them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 26, verse 130:

واذا بطشتم بطشتم جبارین (130)

These people were great rebels and insolent transgressors. When they seized someone in their oppressive grip, they went beyond all limits. Oppression and ruthlessness were their custom, just as every tyrant possessing material power in this world has his own law.

Accordingly, Hazrat Hud invites them to fear God and to submit to obedience to His Messenger, so that Allah and His Messenger might restrain them from this severity.

So fear Allah and obey me. (131)

Hud reminds them that the material strength you possess, and through which you build great palaces and display the awe of your power, is all a blessing granted by Allah. In return for this blessing, the fitting course would have been for you to give thanks to Allah, and to fear that Allah might take this blessing away from you and further punish you for it, since you indulge in extravagance (israf), engage in purposeless activities, and inflict oppression and cruelty.

﴿And fear Him who has provided you with what you know … the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

First, Prophet Hud reminds his people of the blessings they have been given, that they know well what favours they have received. They can see for themselves what they have. They are immersed in that state, yet they also mention some important things by name. He gave them cattle, gave them children, gave them gardens and gave them springs of water. These were the most important factors in the development of that age, while these same things are of fundamental importance in the development of every age and remain important today.

Then he warns these people of the punishment of a tremendous day. Because of the course they had adopted, they had become deserving of punishment. Since Hud was their own brother, he warned them with great compassion and in an extremely heartfelt manner, for through the insight of prophethood the punishment was clearly certain to him.

However, this compassionate advice and warning did not affect their hearts, which had become very hard and were set upon obstinacy and rebellion.

Lesson No. 166: Explanation of the Verses

141 ... to ... 159

﴿Thamud denied the messengers﴾ ... to ... ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾ (135)

These are the same words and the same call that every Messenger presented. Despite differences of language, place, and nation, the Qur'an brings words that are alike from all the Messengers, to show that the mission of all the Messengers had one purpose and one theme, one outlook and one method. It was one principle and one doctrine upon which these missions and these callings were raised: faith in Allah, the sense and fear of His accountability, and obedience to each Messenger.

After this, the Qur'an mentions the particular matters of the people of Thamud that are suitable to the theme of the Surah at this point. Prophet Salih also reminds them of these, saying: Look at the blessings of Allah upon you. These people lived in the region of al-Hijr, between Syria and the Hijaz. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went on the Battle of Tabuk, he, along with his Companions, made a admonishing tour of their land and homes. Prophet Salih says: In view of your deeds, Allah may take these blessings away from you; so fear Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 165–166:

"Do you approach males among the worlds, and leave what your Lord has created for you as your spouses? Rather, you are a transgressing people." (26:165–166)

The people of Lut (Lot) lived in several settlements in the Jordan valley. The sin to which they were addicted is known by the name of the people of Lut (ʿamal qawm Lut): male homosexuality, and the abandonment of sexual relations with women. This was an extremely repugnant deviation from nature, because Allah created men and women, and placed in each a natural attraction (jadhbiyyah) towards the other. This is a creative secret of Allah. In this way Allah arranged the continuity of human life. Allah established this arrangement of procreation through the union of man and woman. This system too is a part of the system that Allah has put into operation throughout this entire universe, which has bound every person and every thing in it together, so that every person and every thing in this universe is in a state of mutual cooperation. As for the act of men having sexual relations with men, such a relationship is purposeless, fruitless and unproductive, and no purpose is fulfilled through it, and this act is contrary both to the law of nature and to the system of nature according to which this universe is running. It is surprising that some dull-minded people find pleasure in this act, whereas true pleasure is that in which there is the attraction of man and woman, and as a result of which the purposes of nature are also fulfilled. Therefore, the act of the people of Lut is an open deviation from nature. Hence the punishment of this people was that they should either be brought back, or be wiped off the face of the earth, because such people have departed from the caravan of humanity and the community of mankind, and they have now given up the purpose for which Allah created them. Moreover, from the natural act of earlier peoples these were born, and through their natural act they were to produce the coming generations.

When Lut called them to abandon this unnatural deviation, and rebuked them for having given up the path that the Lord had created for them, they rebelled against nature and rejected Allah's creative nature. It became evident that they were not prepared to give up this course of theirs, and were not prepared to return to the sunnah of Allah and to nature.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 26, verse 167:

قالوا لئن ……المخرجین (167)

Hazrat Lut (ʿalayhi al-salam) had settled among these people as an outsider from elsewhere. He had come with Hazrat Ibrahim (ʿalayhi al-salam) from Iraq. When Hazrat Ibrahim left his father and his people, and also left his homeland, and crossed the river Jordan and settled on its far side, Hazrat Lut settled among these people. Later, Allah sent Hazrat Lut as a prophet to these very people, so that he might reform the evil deeds that had taken root among the people of Lut. Now, when they do not accept the Hazrat's message, they threaten that if he does not desist, they will drive him out of the land. In other words, they cannot give up that act, so they wish to stop Lut and end the work of the call.

Accordingly, Hazrat Lut, disregarding their threat, declares that he regards their deed as an extremely detestable act. It is a very great filth and degradation.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 172–175:

ثم دمرنا……المنذرین (173)

Some people say that their towns sank and came under the water. Among these towns was one called "Sodom" (سدوم). Experts in the study of ancient remains say that this town lies beneath the waters of the Dead Sea (بحر مروار).

Some scholars of geology (طبقات الارض) hold the view that beneath the Dead Sea there are the ruins of towns that were once filled with population. Experts in archaeology have discovered the remains of a fortress beside this sea, and near that fortress there is an altar (مذبح) on which sacrifices used to be offered.

In any case, the Qur'an has presented the story of the town of Prophet Lot (حضرت لوط) in this manner, and in matters concerning earlier peoples, the Qur'an is the true and authentic source, because among the books of Allah, it alone has been preserved.

At the end, the same commentary is given in the same words that come after every story.

﴿Kadhdhaba Ashab al-Aykah ... Rabb al-'Alamin﴾ (180)

This is the story of Prophet Shu'ayb (peace be upon him). Historically, this event took place before the time of Prophet Musa (peace be upon him). Here, like the other stories, this account has been related solely to draw lessons and admonition.

"Ashab al-Aykah" is probably just another name for the people of Madyan. Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 181–183:

﴿Give full measure, and be not among those who cause loss.﴾ (182)

As has been detailed in Surah al-A'raf and Surah Hud, these people were deficient in measure and weight. When they took from people, they took more than their due, and when they gave to people, they gave less than their due. When receiving, they paid a low price; when giving, they sold at very high prices. It appears that the settlement of these people lay on a trade route through which caravans passed, and these people imposed their will upon those trading caravans. Their messenger was teaching them to deal with justice and equity, for it is a necessary requirement of a pure and sound belief that you also adopt goodness in your dealings. It is not possible that good belief fails to command good action, and that the outlook on right, justice and equity remains silent.

Now Hazrat Shu'ayb (peace be upon him) stirs in their hearts the zeal of taqwa (God-consciousness) and fear of God. He reminds them that there is a Being who has created you, and that this Being is the Creator of all generations.

And even if you are not bewitched, we still do not accept your messengership, because you are merely a man like us. A messenger cannot be a human being; therefore, you are a liar.

This is a challenge from a man who is extremely arrogant, proud and heedless. The idolaters of Makkah likewise made such demands of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Lesson No. 169: At a Glance

Here the stories come to a close. All of these stories were a brief account of the Messengers and their mission. Their peoples repeatedly denied the Messengers, and the nations kept turning away. They issued challenges. Miracles did come, and when they insisted on denial, the punishment of Allah came upon them.

The first lesson of this surah was an introduction, and in it the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was addressed regarding the polytheists of Makkah.

﴿Perhaps you would destroy yourself with grief that they do not believe. If We willed, We could send down upon them a sign from the heaven so that their necks would remain bowed before it. Never does there come to them any new reminder from the Most Merciful except that they turn away from it. They have already denied, so there will soon come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ (26:3-6) After this, the stories were presented, and they were examples of the reports about which the deniers had always mocked.

When the stories ended, the flow of discourse returned to its subject, that is, to the central theme of the surah. This final lesson is, as it were, a comment on the whole surah. It emphasizes that this Qur'an is from the Lord of the worlds. Long periods have passed over these stories, yet the Qur'an presents these events. The scholars of the Children of Israel know the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and also know the Qur'an revealed upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, that it is from Allah, because these are the same events and the same Messenger that are mentioned in the books of the earlier Prophets. But the polytheists of Makkah, despite seeing clear proofs, do not accept it out of obstinacy. They suppose that it is sorcery or poetry. Even if this Qur'an were revealed to a non-Arab and he presented it to them in their own language before them, they would still not believe, because they do not deny it for lack of any proof, but deprived of faith merely because of obstinacy. The reports revealed upon Muhammad ﷺ are not like the satanic inspirations to idols. Nor is this Qur'an any kind of poetry, because poetry has a method known well to poets, and poets are a class that wanders through every valley. They give form to any thought, any feeling, and any inclination. Sometimes good, sometimes bad, this speech is revealed by Allah. It is for the admonition and reminder of the polytheists of Arabia, so that they may take heed before a punishment overtakes them and before those matters that they mock become a reality before them.

﴿And those who have done wrong will soon know to what final turning they will be returned.﴾ (26:228)

[Verses 196–197]

"And indeed it is in the Scriptures of the former peoples. Is it not a sign for them that the scholars of the Children of Israel know it?" (26:196–197)

The praise and mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the creed of Tawhid and the way of life that he presented, were both present in the earlier Scriptures. For this reason, the scholars of the Children of Israel awaited this final Messenger with great eagerness, and they used to wait for "this Messenger." Then many of them would say that the time of "this Messenger" had arrived, and they would speak about him with one another, as has become known through the accounts of Hadrat Salman al-Farisi, Abdullah ibn Salam, and other scholars of the Children of Israel.

They would neither have confirmed it, nor accepted that this Qur'an had been sent down to them. Even such a miraculous proof they would not have granted acceptance.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 202–203:

﴿Then they will say, "Will we be reprieved?"﴾ (26:204)

That is, will we be given another respite in the world so that we may reform? Would that it were so!

The disbelievers of Makkah repeatedly demanded: "Bring that punishment of God with which you frighten us and recount its stories to us, so that we may see it." They mocked religion. Have these people become so bold and arrogant merely because they are prosperous? Luxury has made them dull-witted, and they regard the punishment of God as something unlikely to occur. Their condition is that of people who will eat and drink forever. Such people think that they will always remain as they are; they cannot even conceive of circumstances changing.

Here they are awakened from such heedlessness and told that, at that time, their condition will be such that all the provisions of this world will become useless, and nothing will be able to benefit them.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 26, verses 204–207:

﴿Then is it Our punishment that they seek to hasten?﴾ (26:204)

On the one hand they demand the punishment and seek to hasten it; on the other hand the punishment descends. It appears as though the long life of luxury and ease they were leading was as if it had never been. Throughout that whole life there will be no benefit for them, and no deed in it that could lead to any lightening of their punishment.

In a sound hadith it is related: "The disbeliever will be brought forward and dipped once into the Fire. Then he will be asked, 'Did you ever see any good (and comfort) in your life? Did you ever see any prosperity?' He will say, 'No, by Allah, O Lord, I have seen nothing at all.' Then a person who in the world was in the worst of conditions will be brought forward, and he will be shown one hue of Paradise. Then he will be asked, 'Did you ever see any bad days?' He will say, 'By Allah, O Lord of Majesty, no hardship ever came upon me.'" (Ibn Kathir)

After this they are warned: this warning that is being given to you is because destruction is approaching you very swiftly, and it is part of the mercy of Allah that He does not destroy any town until a messenger has come to it. This is the Sunnah of Allah.

He will say, 'By Allah, O Lord of Majesty, no hardship ever came upon me.'" (Ibn Kathir)

After this they are warned: this warning that is being given to you is because destruction is approaching you very swiftly, and it is part of the mercy of Allah that He does not destroy any town until a messenger has come to it. This is the Sunnah of Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 26, verses 208–209:

﴿And We did not destroy any town except that it had warners,﴾ ﴿as a reminder; and We are never unjust.﴾ (26:208–209)

Allah has taken from humanity a primordial covenant that they will worship Him alone and regard Him as One, without any partner. Human nature by itself acknowledges the existence of the Creator of the universe, provided that corruption and deviation do not arise within it. (Para 9, p. ……) Then Allah placed abundant proofs throughout this universe. All these proofs guide toward the conclusion that the universe has a Creator. If people forget this primordial covenant and do not reflect upon the proofs of faith, then a warner comes to them, who reminds them of this natural lesson and awakens them from the slumber of heedlessness. In this sense, prophethood consists of a reminder and the awakening of people who are asleep. It is the mercy and grace of Allah that He made it binding upon Himself to send messengers, so that We do not punish until We have sent a messenger. When the messenger comes and people still do not believe, do not remember, and do not awaken, this becomes their failure, and they abandon the path of guidance; therefore the punishment becomes due.

Earlier, the Qur'an was described as coming from the Lord of the Worlds and being brought down by the Trustworthy Spirit (Ruh al-Amin). The discourse then moved on to say that these people have become fixed in denial and are hastening the punishment out of their ignorance. However, regarding the Qur'an they also made the accusation that it is a revelation (al-qa') from the devils (shayatin), in the same way that devils cast words (kalimat) into soothsayers (kahin), some of which contain news of the unseen, and by which they set up their trade in soothsaying (kahanat).

Here, however, this claim is refuted: every religion and community knows what the work of Satan is, whereas the Qur'an performs the work of reform and guidance, and Satan, according to the conception of every religion and community, calls to evil, misguidance and error.

Then, where is the power in satanic forces to be able to bring down the Qur'an? The arrangement for the descent of revelation and the Qur'an from Allah is extremely protected. It is brought by the Trustworthy Spirit, by the command of the Lord of the Worlds, with the utmost protection, trustworthiness and integrity.

Now the direction of the address turns to the Noble Messenger (ﷺ). He is warned against shirk, although the occurrence of shirk from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is a far-fetched matter. In reality, through addressing the Messenger, the community is being brought to attention, and he is being instructed to warn his close relatives. Let him rely upon Allah; Allah is always watching over him and protecting him.

"Treat with humility those who follow you, but if they disobey you, say: 'I am free of responsibility for what you do.' And put your trust in the Mighty, the Merciful, who sees you when you rise, and sees your movements among those who prostrate. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."

If the Prophet ﷺ himself were to call upon anyone other than Allah, he too would be among those punished. Although this is impossible, Allah has supposed it for the sake of making the point clear. If this is the case for him, then others are of no consequence whatsoever. Those who call upon other than Allah, night and day, how can they escape the punishment of Allah? Therefore there is no leniency in this matter. Not even the Messenger is exempt from it. If he were to commit this great sin, then ……as well.

After warning the people through the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of the punishment, he is now commanded to warn his own close relatives, so that people from afar may also be more fearful. If the close relatives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ (such as Abu Talib) did not believe and died in polytheism, they would be among those punished, so other people should know that there would be no leniency for them either.

It is narrated in Bukhari and Muslim that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ climbed Mount Safa and called out, "Ya sabahah!" (an Arabic cry used to raise an alarm), and all the people gathered. Everyone rushed to him, or sent a representative. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Banu Abd al-Muttalib, O Banu Murrah, O Banu Lu'ayy! Tell me, if I were to inform you that an army is about to attack you from the other side of this mountain, would you believe me?" They said, "Yes." He said: "I warn you that I am a warner for you, and a severe punishment awaits you." Abu Lahab said: "May you be destroyed all day long! Did you call us only for this?" And at that very occasion this surah was also revealed: "Perish the hands of Abu Lahab, and perish he." Imam Muslim narrated this from Aisha through his chain of narration. She said: When this verse was revealed, "And warn your closest kinsmen" (26:214), the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up and said: "O Fatimah bint Muhammad, O Safiyyah bint Abd al-Muttalib, O children of Abd al-Muttalib, I have no authority on your behalf with Allah. He said: When this verse was revealed and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called the Quraysh, he spoke both generally and specifically. He said: "O people of Quraysh, save yourselves from the Fire. ﴿But if they disobey you, say: "Indeed, I am free of what you do."﴾ (62 : 612)

And put your trust in the Mighty, the Most Merciful, ﴿And put your trust in the Mighty, the Merciful, Who sees you when you stand [in prayer], and your movements among those who prostrate. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.﴾ (62:22). Leave them to their disobedience, declare your disassociation from their deeds, turn to your Lord with reliance upon Him, and seek help from the Most Generous Lord in every matter. Here two attributes of Allah are mentioned, which recur repeatedly in this Surah: the attribute of Might and the attribute of Mercy. That is, He sees you in solitude and He watches you in congregation. That is, when you are among the worshippers, that is, the believers, training them, leading them in prayer, and delivering the sermon to them, Allah oversees your every movement and rest, and He also watches your call to faith and the dangers you face. He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.

In this manner of expression, the aim is to instill in the Prophet (ﷺ) the awareness that Allah is close to him, watching over him, and bestowing His favours upon him. Thus the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) believed that he was under Allah's protection and within the shelter of His mercy. Accordingly, he lived his life in that pleasant and beloved environment.

The devils descend upon liars, impostors, wicked people, and deceitful soothsayers. And it is these soothsayers and misguided religious leaders who bring satanic words, embellish them, and mislead the common people.

﴿Shall I inform you upon whom the devils descend? They descend upon every sinful liar.﴾ (041)

Those who confirmed them were people ready to believe every kind of superstition and every kind of fable. Yet these soothsayers did not call people towards any good, nor did they lead people towards the path of faith. The condition of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was very different from theirs. Through the Qur'an, he called people towards a most solid system of life.

These soothsayers would sometimes say about the Qur'an that it is poetry, and about the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he is a poet. But they were perplexed, because the Qur'an is nonetheless an unparalleled speech, which reaches the hearts of people. It creates a new consciousness within people, and its effects are so deep that the common people cannot reject it.

Therefore, in this surah, the point was clarified that the system the Prophet (ﷺ) presents, and the system the noble Qur'an presents, is not poetic speech or thought. The Qur'an proceeds from beginning to end on one single doctrine and one single method. It has one fixed aim and objective. It moves straight forward towards that objective, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) also follows the same method. It is not that he says one thing today and the opposite tomorrow. He never follows shifting inclinations, tendencies and momentary desires. He brings one call and gives that same call. He presents one creed, and he works according to a method in which there is no crookedness. Poets, however, are not like this. Poets are captives of changing impressions and momentary emotions. Their consciousness governs them, and they express whatever state their consciousness is in. At one moment they see a reality as black and call it black; at the next moment, when it seems beneficial to them, they see it as white and call it white. If they are pleased with someone, they praise him, and if they are displeased, they condemn him. Then every poet has his own temperament and his own poetry.

Furthermore, poets create for themselves a world of their own and get lost within it. They produce certain actions and mental conclusions, and then, taking them as realities, they themselves are affected by them. For this reason such people are not people of action, because they remain lost in their imaginary world.

But the person who rises with a definite call does not have a poetic temperament. The bearer of a definite call wants to see that call established in the real world in practice. Every caller has a definite goal and objective. Moreover, every caller has laid down a method for establishing his call. He proceeds on that defined path towards a defined direction. He does not wander here and there. His vision is sharp, his intellect is alive, and he does not live in the world of illusions and conjectures. Nor is he satisfied merely by drawing an imaginary plan; he wishes to build the practical world upon his plan.

Therefore, there is a fundamental difference between the method of the Messengers and the method of poets, and there is certainly no commonality between the two. This matter is not so complicated that it cannot be understood.

If they are pleased with someone, they praise him, and if they are displeased, they condemn him. Then every poet has his own temperament and his own poetry.

Furthermore, poets create for themselves a world of their own and get lost within it. They produce certain actions and mental conclusions, and then, taking them as realities, they themselves are affected by them. For this reason such people are not people of action, because they remain lost in their imaginary world.

But the person who rises with a definite call does not have a poetic temperament. The bearer of a definite call wants to see that call established in the real world in practice. Every caller has a definite goal and objective. Moreover, every caller has laid down a method for establishing his call. He proceeds on that defined path towards a defined direction. He does not wander here and there. His vision is sharp, his intellect is alive, and he does not live in the world of illusions and conjectures. Nor is he satisfied merely by drawing an imaginary plan; he wishes to build the practical world upon his plan.

Therefore, there is a fundamental difference between the method of the Messengers and the method of poets, and there is certainly no commonality between the two. This matter is not so complicated that it cannot be understood.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 26, verse 227:

إلا الذين ……(721)

"Except for those who believe, do righteous deeds, remember Allah often, and, when they are wronged, defend themselves. And those who do wrong will come to know what final place they will be returned to."

Therefore, the people of faith are not included among those (poets who are misguided). These people believed, and their hearts and minds became filled with Islamic belief and faith. Their lives began to run on a (divine) method (manhaj). In their ordinary lives they began to do righteous deeds, and their powers began to be spent on the path of good deeds and beautiful goodness. They came out of the world of mere illusions and imaginings, and they used their art for their conviction as well. That is, if someone wronged them, they took revenge. That is, they accepted the truth in practice, and their art also came onto the field in its support.

Among such people of art, in the early period of the struggle of tawhid against shirk, in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Hassan ibn Thabit, Ka'b ibn Malik and Abdullah ibn Rawahah (may Allah be pleased with them) were among the poets of the Ansar, and Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ari, Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith ibn Abd al-Muttalib were (poets as well). These two, in the Days of Ignorance, would say whatever they said about the Prophet ﷺ. When they became Muslims and became sincere (in their faith), they displayed great skill in praising the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and defended Islam.

It is found in a authentic hadith that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ instructed Hassan ibn Thabit: "Satirize them, and Jibril is with you." Abd al-Rahman ibn Ka'b narrated from his father that he said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Allah has revealed about poets in verse what He has revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "A believer fights with his sword and also fights with his tongue. By the One in whose hand is my soul, what you shoot at them is like a rain of arrows." (Imam Ahmad)

Islamic poetry and art can be produced in various styles. That is, this is one form which came into existence at the beginning of Islam and at that time it was also needed; but in accordance with the Islamic concept of life, there are also many other domains of poetry and speech which Islam permits.

It is not necessary that Islamic art must be only that which is in defence of Islam, or in which the call to Islam is directly present, or in which Islam is praised, the Prophet of Islam is praised, the great figures of Islam are eulogized, or the praise of Allah is recited. It is not necessary that a poem on these subjects is Islamic, and if it is not on these subjects it is not Islamic. A poetic glance at the turning of night and day, and a glance at the scenes of the universe through which a Muslim's consciousness and imagination perceive the power of God, is genuine Islamic art. The truth is that a moment in which the wisdom of Allah becomes illuminated upon a person's heart and mind, and in which a person perceives the wonders of this universe, is in such moments that Islamic literature is created.

The distinction between Islamic art and non-Islamic art is that Islam has its own concept of life, and Islamic society has a particular form of relationships. If any art is created on the basis of Islamic concepts, Islamic relationships and Islamic morality, then it is Islamic and Islam approves of it; otherwise it is not.

And the surah concludes with this threat and general warning:

"And those who do wrong will come to know what final place they will be returned to." The theme of this whole surah has been this, and in it the picture of the enmity and obstinacy of the polytheists has been drawn. It was shown that they persisted in rebellion against Allah's warning, and rather, in the world of pride, they kept demanding the speedy descent of punishment. Also, in this surah a picture of the punishments that descended upon all such people has been drawn, and the outcomes of various messengers have been shown.

Therefore, at the end of the surah, the opposing forces of the Prophet ﷺ were summarily made to understand that they too should take care of their own welfare, for they are about to face a fate of their own. As it were, this is the final blow upon the mental world of the Meccan disbelievers, and it is in words such that each person's thought can grasp its meaning according to his capacity. Thus, this is an earthquake in the palace of the polytheists, brought about at the end of the surah.
